content:
Each cerebral hemisphere can be divided into sections, or lobes, each of which specializes in different functions. To understand each lobe and its specialty, we will take a tour of the cerebral hemispheres.

The most important parts of our brain

Cerebral Cortex
The cerebral cortex surrounds the cerebrum and has many folds. Due to its large surface area, the cerebral cortex accounts for 50% of the brain's total weight. Coating the surface of the cerebrum and the cerebellum is a vital layer of tissue the thickness of a stack of two or three dimes. It is called the cortex, from the Latin word for bark. Most of the actual information processing in the brain takes place in the cerebral cortex. When people talk about "gray matter" in the brain, they are talking about the cortex. The cortex is gray because nerves in this area lack the insulation that makes most other parts of the brain appear to be white. The folds in the brain add to its surface area and therefore increase the amount of gray matter and the volume of information that can be processed.

Frontal Lobes

Frontal Lobes

The two frontal lobes lie directly behind the forehead. When you plan a schedule, imagine the future, or use reasoned arguments, these two lobes do much of the work. One of the ways the frontal lobes seem to do these things is by acting as short-term storage sites, allowing one idea to be kept in mind while other ideas are considered. After a brain injury in 1848, Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe, but his personality completely changed! This helped scientists learn that the frontal lobes control personality, decision-making, and impulse control.

Motor Cortex

Motor Cortex

In the back portion of each frontal lobe is a motor cortex, which helps plan, control, and execute voluntary movement, like moving your arm or kicking a ball. The motor cortex is organized like a "homunculus," a tiny distorted human figure where body parts that require more precise control (like hands and lips) take up more space in the brain.

Parietal Lobes

Parietal Lobes

When you enjoy a good meal the taste, smell, and texture of the food two sections behind the frontal lobes called the parietal lobes are at work. Your parietal lobes play a huge role in spatial awareness and navigation. Ever walked through your house in the dark without bumping into everything? That’s your parietal lobes working behind the scenes! They help your brain understand where your body is in space, making things like driving, catching a ball, or even reaching for your coffee cup feel effortless.

Somatosensory Cortex

Somatosensory Cortex

The forward parts of these lobes, just behind the motor areas, is the somatosensory cortex. These areas receive information about temperature, taste, touch (pain) , and movement from the rest of the body. People who lose a limb sometimes experience phantom limb sensations because their somatosensory cortex still thinks the missing limb is there! This happens because the brain rewires itself but keeps old sensory maps.

Occipital Lobes

Occipital Lobes

As you look at the words and pictures on this page, two areas at the back of the brain are at work. These lobes, called the occipital lobes, process images from the eyes and link that information with images stored in memory. Damage to the occipital lobes can cause blindness. In some cases, blind individuals experience blindsight, where they can respond to visual stimuli (like detecting movement) without actually "seeing" it. This happens because some visual information bypasses conscious awareness and still gets processed!

Temporal Lobes

Temporal Lobes

The last lobes on our tour of the cerebral hemispheres are the temporal lobes, which lie in front of the visual areas and nest under the parietal and frontal lobes. Whether you appreciate symphonies or rock music, your brain responds through the activity of these lobes. At the top of each temporal lobe is an area responsible for receiving information from the ears. The underside of each temporal lobe plays a crucial role in forming and retrieving memories, including those associated with music. Other parts of this lobe integrate memories and sensations of taste, sound, sight, and touch.

Inner Brain

Inner Brain

Deep within the brain, hidden from view, lie structures that are the gatekeepers between the spinal cord and the cerebral hemispheres. These structures not only determine our emotional state, but they also modify our perceptions and responses and allow us to initiate movements that without thinking about them. Like the lobes in the cerebral hemispheres, the structures described below come in pairs: each is duplicated in the opposite half of the brain.

The hypothalamus, about the size of a pearl, directs a multitude of important functions. It wakes you up in the morning and gets the adrenaline flowing during a test or job interview. The hypothalamus is also an important emotional center, controlling the chemicals that make you feel exhilarated, angry, or unhappy. Near the hypothalamus lies the thalamus, a major clearinghouse for information going to and from the spinal cord and the cerebrum.

An arching tract of nerve cells leads from the hypothalamus and the thalamus to the hippocampus. This tiny nub acts as a memory indexer—sending memories out to the appropriate part of the cerebral hemisphere for long-term storage and retrieving them when necessary. The basal ganglia (not shown) are clusters of nerve cells surrounding the thalamus. They are responsible for initiating and integrating movements. Parkinson’s disease, which results in tremors, rigidity, and a stiff, shuffling walk, affects the nerve cells in the basal ganglia.

title: Facts about our brain
about:
We Don't Just Use 10% of Our Brains.

content:
We Don't Just Use 10% of Our Brains.
Have you ever heard that we just use 10% of our brains? It's an oft-cited statistic, but constant repetition does not make it accurate. People often use this inaccurate stat to imply that the mind is capable of much greater things, such as dramatically increased intelligence, psychic abilities, or even telekinesis. If the 10% number were true, brain damage would be far less likely—after all, we would only have to worry about that tiny 10% of our brains being injured.

Brain Damage Isn't Always Permanent

Brain damage by an injury

The brain is fragile and can be damaged by things such as injury, stroke, or disease. This damage can result in a range of consequences, from mild disruptions in cognitive abilities to complete impairment. Brain damage can be devastating, but is it always permanent? A person's ability to recover from brain damage depends upon the severity and the location of the injury. For example, a blow to the head during a football game might lead to a concussion. While the injury can be quite serious, most people can recover when given time to heal. A severe stroke, on the other hand, can result in damage that can very well be permanent. However, it is important to remember that the human brain has an impressive amount of plasticity. Even following a serious brain event, such as a stroke, it is possible for the brain to partially or fully heal itself over time and form new connections.

People Aren't Fully Right- or Left-Brained
Have you ever heard someone describe themselves as either left-brained or right-brained? This idea stems from the popular notion that people are either dominated by their right or left brain hemispheres. According to this idea, people who are "right-brained" are believed to be more creative and expressive, while those who are "left-brained" are positioned as more analytical and logical.

Humans Don't Have the Biggest Brains
The human brain is quite large in proportion to human body size, but humans don't have the largest brains of any organism. How big is the human brain? How does it compare to other species? The average adult brain weighs about 3 pounds and measures about 15 centimeters in length. The largest animal brain belongs to that of a sperm whale, weighing in at a whopping 18 pounds! Another large-brained animal is the elephant, with an average brain size of around 11 pounds (5 kilograms). But what about relative brain size in proportion to body size? Though the proportion of the human brain to the human body is larger than many animals, the notion that it's the largest is also inaccurate. Surprisingly, one animal with a larger brain-to-body weight ratio than humans is the shrew, with a brain that makes up about 10% of its body mass.

New Brain Cells May Form Throughout Life
Traditional wisdom has long suggested that adults only have so many brain cells and that we never form new ones. Once these cells are lost, are they gone for good? Experts have uncovered evidence that the human adult brain does indeed form new cells throughout life, even during old age.

Alcohol Can Affect Your Brain Cells
Partly related to the misconception that we never grow new neurons is the idea that drinking alcohol can lead to cell death in the brain. Drink too much or too often, some people might warn, and you'll lose precious brain cells that you can never get back. Could drinking alcohol really kill brain cells? Researchers don't believe that alcohol use actually kills brain cells, though evidence does suggest that it can inhibit new cell growth. Additionally, long-term use can have a significant impact on brain functioning.

There Are About 85 Billion Neurons in the Human Brain
An often-cited statistic is that there are 100 billion neurons in the human brain. This number has been repeated so often and for so long that no one is completely sure where it originated. In 2009, however, one researcher decided to count neurons in adult brains and found that the number was just a bit off the mark.Based on this research, it appears that the human brain contains closer to 85 billion neurons. So while 100 billion is a few billion too high, 85 billion is still nothing to sneeze at.

Using Learning Styles Isn't Necessarily Effective

Learning styles suggest that each person has a preferred learning style that helps them learn best. For example, one popular theory proposes that people tend to be more auditory, visual, or kinesthetic learners. In other words, some people learn best by hearing, seeing, or doing. While it's an appealing concept, there's little research to suggest that learning based on your preferred style actually has any impact on learning outcomes. One large-scale study found no evidence to support the use of learning style assessment instruments.

Myths about the brain

content:
The brain is the central control of the entire body. It is part of the nervous system, which contains the spinal cord and a dense network of nerves and neurons. They work together as a machine that controls all activities of the body, from sensory functions to various actions. When the brain is damaged, it can affect various aspects, from memory and sensation to individual personality. Brain disorders include causes or factors that affect the brain, such as:

Diseases

Genetics

Aging

Injuries

Mental health disorders are very common. According to the National Institute of Mental Health, about 20% of the population has mental health disorders. The risk of developing a disorder is higher in the following cases:

Family history of the disease

Experiencing trauma or stress

History of alcohol or drug addiction

Brain injuries

According to the U.S. National Library of Medicine, there are more than 600 mental disorders. Common mental disorders include epilepsy, learning disabilities, neuromuscular disorders, autism, ADHD, cerebral palsy, and many other conditions that we cannot cover in detail here.

An overview of the most common brain diseases

Conditions
General explanation

Alzheimer's Disease

A progressive neurodegenerative disorder that causes memory loss, confusion, and changes in behavior. It’s the most common form of dementia.

Dementia

A broad term for a group of symptoms affecting memory, thinking, and social abilities, often caused by various diseases like Alzheimer’s.

Brain Cancer

Uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in the brain, which can form tumors that interfere with brain function, causing headaches, seizures, and cognitive issues.

Epilepsy 

A neurological disorder marked by recurrent, unprovoked seizures due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Seizures can vary in severity and type.

Mental health disorders

Conditions that affect thinking, feeling, behavior, or mood, such as depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia. These can interfere with daily functioning and well-being.

Parkinson's disease

A progressive neurodegenerative condition that affects movement, causing tremors, stiffness, and slow movement. Other movement disorders may include conditions like Huntington’s disease.

Stroke & TIA

A stroke occurs when blood flow to the brain is interrupted, leading to brain cell death. A TIA, often called a "mini-stroke," is a temporary blockage that doesn’t cause lasting damage but signals a higher risk of a full stroke.

In this course, we will study the most common mental health disorders in unit 7

We need our brain!

Disorders and Genetics
Most neurological disorders have a very high genetic factor. The heritability of diseases such as bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and autism can reach up to 80% or even higher. This figure is significantly higher when compared to other hereditary diseases such as breast cancer or Parkinson's. If a family member has one of these conditions, the risk for subsequent generations is very high.

Sometimes inheritance occurs when either the father or the mother has the disease, but sometimes neither parent has it, yet the child still develops the condition. Most mental disorders result from a complex combination of genetics and environmental factors. Environmental factors such as pollution, unhealthy diets, stress in the work environment, social interactions, family medical history, educational environment, and personal history can all have an impact.

A Personal Story
We are all growing older, every year, every month, every day, even every second. Aging is an inevitable part of life. But getting older isn’t just about physical changes; it also means mental and neurological transformations. For many, this includes facing conditions like dementia, a cruel disorder that slowly erodes memory, personality, and independence. One of my closest friends, now 86 years old, is battling this reality. At first, the signs were subtle, occasionally forgetting a name or misplacing a note. But over time, the symptoms became undeniable. His once vivid stories turned fragmented and confused. Then, not long ago, I received a phone call from the police.

This kind-hearted man, one of the most honest people I know, had gone to the store. Absentmindedly, he placed an item in his pocket. At the checkout, he had no recollection of doing so. The store staff noticed and, following protocol, called the police. Of course, they quickly understood they weren’t dealing with a criminal, just an elderly man struggling with a fading memory. Yet, for him, it was an overwhelming and distressing experience.It is heartbreaking to witness dementia take hold of my dear friend. Our visits have changed. Now, we watch children’s cartoons, sing simple songs, and do activities like finger painting. Seeing him like this is painful. But when I look over and see a bright, childlike smile on his face as we watch a cartoon together, my heart swells. In that moment, I know he is happy.

I cannot change his reality. I cannot bring back the pieces of him that have faded. But I can be there, accepting the moment for what it is, cherishing the joy that still exists. Sometimes, that’s all we can do.

Career opportunities for elderly coaches in Vietnam are growing due to the rising elderly population and a gap in mental health services for seniors. As life expectancy increases, the demand for professionals to support the elderly, particularly in mental well-being and life adjustments, is on the rise. Key Points
All countries face significant challenges in ensuring that their healthcare and social systems are prepared to make the most of this demographic shift.

By 2050, 80% of the population in low- and middle-income countries will be elderly.

The rate of population aging is much faster than before.

In 2020, the number of people aged 60 and over exceeded the number of children under five years old.

From 2015 to 2050, the proportion of the global population over 60 years old will nearly double, from 12% to 22%.

One in four older adults experiences mental health issues. The most common problems are depression, dementia, and anxiety.

Depression and dementia are the most prevalent conditions, affecting 5% to 7% of people over 60 years old.

Anxiety ranks second, with the World Health Organization (WHO) reporting that it affects 3.8% of older adults.

content:
Although aging itself is not a disease, it is a risk factor for various medical conditions. This does not mean that you will necessarily develop an age-related disease; it simply means that you are more likely to encounter these conditions as you grow older. Physiological processes such as inflammation, exposure to pollutants and radiation (such as ultraviolet radiation from the sun), lifestyle factors like smoking, diet, and exercise, as well as general wear and tear, can all accelerate the aging process in different individuals. Numerous research projects worldwide are being conducted to determine the effects of aging on the human body, aiming to distinguish which conditions are an inevitable result of aging and which can be prevented. Symptoms of mental disorders in the elderly include:

1
Noticeable changes in mood, energy levels, or appetite

2
Feeling depressed or struggling to feel positive emotions

3
Difficulty sleeping or sleeping too much

4
Trouble concentrating, feeling restless, or tense

5
Increased anxiety or stress

6
Significant changes in sleep patterns

7
Anger, irritability, or aggression

8
Persistent headaches, digestive problems, or pain

9
Substance or alcohol abuse

10
Feelings of sadness or hopelessness

11
Thoughts of death or suicide

12
Behaviors that negatively affect work, family, or social life

How to Help and support the Elderly
Supporting elderly individuals with their struggles as a coach involves a combination of empathy, active listening, and providing tailored strategies to improve their mental, physical, and emotional well-being. Here are some key ways to support them:

Active Listening: Take the time to listen to their concerns and challenges without judgment. Acknowledge their feelings and provide a safe space for them to express themselves.

Empathy and Patience: Understand that aging can bring about physical, mental, and emotional challenges. Approach them with patience, kindness, and empathy, which helps build trust and a strong coach-client relationship.

Promote Social Interaction: Encourage social activities to prevent isolation, such as connecting with family, friends, or local community groups. Social engagement can improve mental health and overall well-being.

Cognitive Stimulation: Provide activities that challenge their cognitive abilities, like puzzles, games, or learning new skills. This helps with memory retention and mental sharpness.

Physical Activity: Help them incorporate safe and appropriate physical exercises into their daily routine. Physical activity can reduce the risk of illness, improve mobility, and boost mood.

Emotional Support: Be there to provide emotional guidance, particularly for elderly individuals dealing with anxiety, depression, or the loss of loved ones. Encourage them to express their feelings and provide coping strategies.

Personalized Goal Setting: Work with them to set realistic, achievable goals that promote a sense of purpose and accomplishment. These goals could relate to maintaining health, building new skills, or improving daily independence.

Promote Independence: Support them in maintaining or regaining independence in daily tasks, such as personal hygiene, mobility, or cooking. Empowering them to do things on their own, with some guidance, helps preserve their dignity and confidence.

Memory

content:
Dementia is a syndrome, typically chronic or progressive, characterized by a deterioration in cognitive function (i.e., the ability to process thought) that exceeds what is expected from normal aging. It affects:

Memory

Thinking

Orientation

Comprehension

Calculation

Learning capacity

Language

Judgment

The feeling of being lost

Importantly, consciousness remains unaffected. Cognitive impairment is often accompanied, and sometimes preceded, by deterioration in emotional control, social behavior, or motivation. Dementia arises from various diseases and injuries that primarily or secondarily affect the brain, such as Alzheimer’s disease or stroke. It is one of the leading causes of disability and dependency among older individuals worldwide. The condition impacts not only those affected but also their carers and families, often leading to stigma and barriers to diagnosis and care. Its effects on caregivers and society can be physical, psychological, social, and economic.

Rates of Dementia Globally

Approximately 50 million people have dementia.

Nearly 60% of these individuals live in low- and middle-income countries.

Annually, there are 10 million new cases.

Among the general population aged 60 and above, dementia prevalence is estimated at 5–8%.

Symptoms of Dementia
Dementia affects individuals differently, depending on the disease's impact and the person’s personality before the illness. Symptoms are categorized into three stages: Early stage, often overlooked due to its gradual onset. Middle stage, symptoms become more apparent and restrictive. Late stage involves near-total dependence and inactivity. 

Early Stage

1
Forgetfulness

2
Losing track of time

3
Becoming lost in familiar places

Middle Stage

1
Forgetfulness of recent events and names

2
Getting lost at home

3
Increasing difficulty with communication

4
Requiring help with personal care

5
Behavioral changes, such as wandering or repeated questioning

Late Stage

1
Loss of awareness of time and place

2
Difficulty recognizing relatives and friends

3
Increased need for assisted self-care

4
Difficulty walking

5
Behavioral changes, such as aggression

Treatment and Care

Currently, there is no cure or treatment available to stop the progression of dementia. However, research into new treatments is ongoing. Despite this, various interventions can support and improve the quality of life for people with dementia and their caregivers. The primary goals of dementia care include: Early diagnosis to enable optimal management, Optimizing physical health, cognition, activity, and well-being, Identifying and treating physical illnesses and Detecting and managing challenging behavioral and psychological symptoms

Promote Social Interaction

Advice for Caregivers
Supporting someone with dementia requires patience, understanding, and proactive communication. Here are some tips:

Set a Positive Mood for Interaction - Approach with kindness and positivity.

Get the Person’s Attention - Reduce distractions and maintain eye contact.

State Your Message Clearly - Use simple language and a calm tone.

Ask Simple, Answerable Questions - For example, yes-or-no questions when possible.

Listen Actively - Pay attention with your ears, eyes, and heart.

Break Activities into Manageable Steps - Guide them through tasks one step at a time.

Distract and Redirect When Challenges Arise - Shift focus when a task becomes too frustrating.

By adopting these strategies, caregivers can foster a more supportive and compassionate environment for those living with dementia.

title: Alzheimer’s Disease
about: Alzheimer’s disease is an age-related condition characterized by memory loss caused by brain shrinkage and the gradual death of brain cells. It is the most common cause of dementia, leading to continuous deterioration in thinking, behavior, and social skills, which severely impac
content:
Alzheimer’s disease is an age-related condition characterized by memory loss caused by brain shrinkage and the gradual death of brain cells. It is the most common cause of dementia, leading to continuous deterioration in thinking, behavior, and social skills, which severely impacts a person’s daily life.

In the United States, approximately 5.8 million people over the age of 65 are affected, with 80% of these individuals aged 75 and older.

Globally, around 50 million people have dementia, with 60–70% diagnosed with Alzheimer’s

Early signs of Alzheimer’s include forgetting recent events or conversations. As the disease progresses, patients experience severe memory loss and lose the ability to perform daily tasks. While there is no cure, medications can temporarily improve symptoms and slow the progression, helping patients maintain their independence for as long as possible. Care programs and support services are available to assist patients and their families. In advanced stages, complications such as dehydration, malnutrition, and infections can arise, often leading to death. The symptoms of Alzheimer’s vary in severity as the disease progresses:

Early Symptoms:

1
Forgetting recent events or conversations

2
Difficulty organizing thoughts or remembering details

Advanced Symptoms:

1
Severe memory loss

2
Difficulty recognizing family or friends

3
Challenges in performing daily activities

4
Behavioral and emotional changes

Symptoms of Alzheimer

Causes of Alzheimer’s Disease
Causes of Alzheimer’s DiseaseIn the early stages, patients may struggle to recall events or articulate thoughts. As the disease progresses, these symptoms worsen, often becoming more noticeable to family and friends. The exact cause of Alzheimer’s remains unknown, but researchers have linked the disease to the following:

Abnormal Brain Proteins:

These proteins disrupt brain cell function, leading to a chain reaction that damages neurons.

Over time, brain cells lose connections and die, hindering nerve signal transmission.

Brain Cell Damage:

The progression is slow, with brain cells dying over several years.

Damage typically begins in the brain's memory centers and may lead to brain shrinkage in later stages.

Scientists believe Alzheimer’s results from a combination of genetic, lifestyle, and environmental factors that negatively impact the brain over time.

How to Prevent Alzheimer’s Disease
Although Alzheimer’s cannot be entirely prevented, lifestyle changes can help reduce the risk. Experts suggest the following:

Dancing is always good for mental health. 

Healthy Lifestyle Choices And Brain-Stimulating Activities:

1
Exercise Regularly: Engage in activities like walking, swimming, or cycling.

2
Follow a Balanced Diet: Include fresh produce, vitamins, and fiber while avoiding processed and fried foods.

3
Manage Health Conditions: Control high blood pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol.

4
Avoid Smoking and Alcohol: These habits can negatively impact brain health.

5
Participating in social events

6
Reading books or newspapers

7
Dancing, playing games, or creating art

By adopting these heart-healthy and mentally stimulating habits, individuals can reduce their risk of developing Alzheimer’s and other forms of dementia.

title: Parkinson’s Disease
about: Parkinson’s disease is a neurological disorder caused by the degeneration of the central nervous system, leading to the deterioration of brain cells and a deficiency of dopamine. Dopamine, a chemical produced by nerve cells, plays a critical role in controlling body movements. In
content:
Parkinson’s disease is a neurological disorder caused by the degeneration of the central nervous system, leading to the deterioration of brain cells and a deficiency of dopamine. Dopamine, a chemical produced by nerve cells, plays a critical role in controlling body movements. In Parkinson’s, the nerve cells responsible for producing dopamine die off, resulting in decreased dopamine levels, which causes the symptoms of the disease. While the exact cause of this nerve cell loss is unknown, experts believe it is due to a combination of genetic and environmental factors.

Parkinson Disease

Main Symptoms of Parkinson’s Disease
Parkinson’s symptoms can manifest physically and cognitively. Symptoms include:

1
Tremors
These can occur not only in the hands and feet but also in the lips and tongue.

2
Slowed Movement
A gradual loss of movement speed and fluidity.

3
Muscle and Bone Stiffness
A lack of flexibility, often accompanied by rigidity.

4
Poor Balance
Difficulty maintaining stability.

5
Loss of Sense of Smell
A diminished or absent ability to detect odors.

6
Sleep Disturbances
Trouble falling or staying asleep.

7
Memory Problems
Issues with recall and cognition.

8
Depression and Irritability
Emotional changes often linked to the disease’s progression.

Risk and Treatment for Parkinson’s Disease
Parkinson’s primarily affects individuals over the age of 50, but in some cases, symptoms can develop in people under 40. The condition is more prevalent in men than in women.While there is no cure for Parkinson’s disease, treatments can help manage symptoms and improve the quality of life. Common treatments include:

Physical Therapy and Speech Therapy: Helps with mobility, speaking, and swallowing.

Medication: Drugs such as levodopa can help replenish dopamine levels.

Surgery: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) may be recommended in severe cases.

Managing Early Stages:
In the early stages, symptoms may be mild, and treatment might not be necessary. Regular health check-ups can help monitor progression and manage symptoms effectively.

Progression of the Disease:
Over time, Parkinson’s can worsen, making daily activities increasingly challenging. Many patients respond well to treatment, experiencing only mild to moderate limitations. However, some may not respond as effectively and could face severe disabilities.

7 Symptoms

Prognosis and Quality of Life
Parkinson’s disease is not fatal but can cause significant difficulties in daily living. In some cases, patients may be at risk of life-threatening complications, such as infections. Early treatment and symptom management are key to helping most patients lead a normal or near-normal life.

content:
Case Study: Nam and His Struggle with Dementia

Nam is a 72-year-old retired literature teacher who lives with his wife, Lan, in Da Nang. He has two grown children Mai, 38, who lives nearby and visits every weekend, and Phong, 41, who works in Ho Chi Minh City and can only visit once every few months. Nam used to be a highly social and active man, often attending community events and volunteering at the local library.

About three years ago, the family noticed subtle changes in Nam’s memory. At first, he would occasionally forget where he left his glasses or call Mai by Phong’s name. The family dismissed it as normal aging. However, over the past year, his condition has worsened significantly. Nam has started to forget recent events completely, like whether he had eaten lunch, or conversations he had the day before. He sometimes becomes disoriented, forgetting the way back home even on familiar streets.

Lan and Mai have also noticed personality changes. Nam, once patient and cheerful, now gets easily frustrated and sometimes withdraws from conversations. He occasionally accuses Lan of moving his belongings or hiding things, which hurts her deeply. On some nights, he wanders the house, unable to sleep, and in the morning he cannot recall why he was awake.

The family feels heartbroken and overwhelmed. Lan is exhausted from constantly supervising her husband, fearing he might leave the house and get lost. Mai struggles to balance supporting her parents with caring for her own children. Phong feels helpless living far away, and every visit leaves him with the painful impression that his father is “disappearing” bit by bit.

They have taken Nam to the doctor, and he has been diagnosed with moderate dementia. The doctor provided some medication to help slow the progression, but the emotional toll on the family remains immense. They are grieving the gradual loss of the man they once knew, and they don’t know how to help or support him beyond meeting his daily needs.

How a Life Coach Can Help the Family

While a life coach cannot treat dementia, they can play an important role in supporting the family as they navigate this difficult journey. Here’s how:

Emotional Support and Coping Strategies

A life coach can provide a safe space for family members to share their grief, frustration, and fears.

They can guide Lan, Mai, and Phong to recognize and process the emotional impact of caregiving, reducing feelings of guilt and helplessness.

Family Communication and Collaboration

The coach can help the family develop better communication and coordination strategies.

For example, creating a shared caregiving schedule, dividing responsibilities, and setting up regular family check-ins can help reduce the burden on Lan and allow Phong to contribute meaningfully even from a distance.

Setting Realistic Expectations

Life coaching can help the family understand that dementia progresses over time, and that expecting Nam to “return to normal” may lead to disappointment.

Instead, the coach can guide them to focus on achievable goals, like maintaining his comfort, safety, and moments of connection.

Practical Guidance for Daily Life

A life coach can offer strategies to make caregiving less stressful, such as establishing daily routines, labeling items in the house, or using reminders to help Nam feel more secure.

Encouraging the family to include meaningful activities—like listening to Nam’s favorite music or looking at old family photos—can strengthen emotional bonds.

Self-Care and Resilience for Caregivers

Caring for someone with dementia is emotionally draining. A coach can help family members prioritize their own health, schedule breaks, and seek support groups or community resources.

By maintaining their own well-being, they can better support Nam in the long term.

With the guidance of a life coach, Nam’s family can learn to navigate the emotional and practical challenges of dementia care. While the disease may continue to progress, the family can find ways to maintain meaningful connections, reduce stress, and face the journey with greater resilience and compassion.

Career opportunities: Promising
Career opportunities as a sex coach in Vietnam are promising. This field is relatively new, and due to a lack of education on the subject, many people have questions and concerns. As a sex coach, your primary role is to assist couples by providing guidance and information. The two most common issues that arise are painful or impossible sex, and couples who no longer engage in intimacy because the passion has faded. As a coach, you help couples address these challenges, offering support to improve their relationships and sexual well-being.

Key Points
Sexuality involves how people experience and express themselves sexually, including physical, emotional, and psychological aspects. A healthy sexual experience requires mutual respect, clear communication, and consent.

Male sex problems include erectile dysfunction, where men struggle to maintain an erection, and performance anxiety, which can cause fear of sexual inadequacy and difficulty during intercourse.

For women, vaginismus is when muscle contractions make penetration painful, while low libido can be caused by hormonal changes or stress. Dyspareunia, or pain during sex, is another common concern.

In relationships, good communication is key to maintaining intimacy. Openly discussing desires, boundaries, and concerns helps strengthen both emotional and sexual connections.

LGBTQ+ individuals often face stigma and discrimination, which can affect mental health. Understanding sexual orientations, such as gay, lesbian, or bisexual, and supporting diverse gender identities, like transgender, is vital for creating an inclusive environment.

title: What is Sexuality?
about: Most of what we know about the physiological mechanisms underlying sexual behavior and motivation comes from animal research. The hypothalamus plays a critical role in motivated behaviors, including sexuality. Specifically, damage to the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus c
content:
Most of what we know about the physiological mechanisms underlying sexual behavior and motivation comes from animal research. The hypothalamus plays a critical role in motivated behaviors, including sexuality. Specifically, damage to the medial preoptic area of the hypothalamus completely disrupts the ability of male rats to engage in sexual behavior. However, it does not affect their effort to access a female ready for mating, suggesting that the ability to engage in sexual behavior and the motivation to do so are regulated by distinct neural systems.

Animal studies indicate that limbic system structures, such as the amygdala and nucleus accumbens, are particularly important for sexual motivation. Damage to these areas reduces sexual motivation but does not impair the ability to perform sexual behavior. Similar dissociations between sexual motivation and capability have been observed in female rats. Research suggests parallels between animals and humans. For instance, the use of erectile dysfunction medications and disorders associated with abnormal hypothalamic function indicate that sexual motivation and the ability to perform may also be separable in humans. Hormones, particularly testosterone, play a significant role in sexual motivation and behavior across many species, though human sexual motivation is less hormonally dependent.

A couple, totally in love ;)

Sexual Orientation
Sexual orientation refers to an individual’s emotional and sexual attraction to others. While most people identify as heterosexual, around 8–10% of the population identifies as homosexual. Research has shown that family circumstances and experiences are very similar between heterosexual and homosexual individuals, dispelling earlier misconceptions about socialization being a primary cause of sexual orientation differences.

The Masters and Johnson Study
In 1966, William Masters and Virginia Johnson published groundbreaking research on the physiological responses during sexual behavior. Unlike earlier studies that relied on interviews and surveys, Masters and Johnson directly observed individuals engaging in sexual activities. They recorded physiological data, including blood pressure, respiration rate, vaginal lubrication, and penile erection.

From their findings, they identified four stages of the sexual response cycle:

1
Excitement
Initial arousal marked by penile or clitoral erection, and vaginal lubrication.

2
Plateau
Increased physiological arousal; men achieve full erection, and women experience swelling and increased blood flow.

3
Orgasm
Rhythmic pelvic contractions in both sexes; ejaculation occurs in men.

4
Resolution
A return to an unaroused state with relaxation. Men experience a refractory period, which varies in length and increases with age.

Masters and Johnson’s research also dispelled myths, such as the belief that penis size is linked to sexual satisfaction, and provided insights into the elasticity of the vagina.

Gender Identity
Gender identity refers to an individual’s internal sense of being male, female, or another gender. While gender identity often aligns with biological sex, this is not always the case. Individuals experiencing gender dysphoria feel significant discomfort with the gender assigned to them at birth. According to the DSM-5, gender dysphoria must persist for at least six months and cause significant distress to be diagnosed.

Many individuals with gender dysphoria take steps to align their physical appearance with their gender identity, including:

1
Cross-dressing and living as their identified gender.

2
Gender-affirming hormone therapy to alter physical traits.

3
Surgical interventions to align external anatomy with their gender identity.

For individuals with gender dysphoria, these changes address a deep-seated sense that their physical body does not align with their true self.

title: Male Sexual Problems
about: Sexual dysfunction issues are common, sometimes affecting more than half of couples. While sexual dysfunction rarely poses a threat to physical health, it can have severe psychological consequences, leading to depression, anxiety, and emotional distress due to feelings of depriva
content:
Sexual dysfunction issues are common, sometimes affecting more than half of couples. While sexual dysfunction rarely poses a threat to physical health, it can have severe psychological consequences, leading to depression, anxiety, and emotional distress due to feelings of deprivation. Men's sexual problems, particularly erectile dysfunction, can also increase the risk of vascular diseases, so it is essential to discuss these issues with a doctor.

Main Types of Sexual Dysfunction in Men:

Erectile Dysfunction (ED)
Sometimes called impotence, this is the inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for sexual activity.

Premature Ejaculation (PE)
The inability to delay orgasm and ejaculation, occurring too soon during intercourse, leaving the partner unsatisfied.

Male Orgasmic Disorder
The inability to reach orgasm with a partner; difficulty achieving orgasm without prolonged intercourse; or inability to climax during intercourse. In some cases, orgasm can only be achieved through masturbation or oral sex.

Inhibited or Decreased Sexual Desire
A lack of interest in sexual activity or a complete absence of sexual desire.

Retrograde Ejaculation
Instead of exiting through the penis, semen moves backward into the bladder during orgasm. This condition is not dangerous and is often a side effect of certain medications.

Priapism
A prolonged erection that is not related to sexual desire. This rare condition is painful, potentially dangerous, and requires immediate medical attention. Call your doctor if you experience this.

If your sexual problem occurs only in specific situations or with certain partners, your condition is considered "situational" rather than "generalized" (which occurs regardless of circumstances or partners). Many of these sexual conditions will occur at some point in a man's life. In fact, some researchers only consider diagnosing sexual dysfunction if the issue happens in 25% of total sexual encounters.

Treatment options

What Causes Sexual Problems in Men?
Since sexual response is complex and involves multiple factors, the causes of sexual dysfunction can be both physical and psychological. Erections rely on the nervous system, vascular system (arteries and veins), and hormone levels, so problems in any of these areas can disrupt sexual function.

Common Physical Causes of Sexual Problems:

1
Conditions or behaviors that increase vascular disease risk, such as smoking, high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, obesity, or medications for these conditions.

2
Diabetes, especially Type 2 diabetes.

3
Hypogonadism, where the testes do not produce enough testosterone.

4
Thyroid disorders (both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism).

5
Adrenal gland disorders, such as Cushing’s syndrome.

6
Noncancerous pituitary growths, which increase levels of the hormone prolactin.

7
Diseases affecting the nervous system, including stroke, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, long-term diabetes, and Parkinson’s disease.

8
Damage to arteries or veins after pelvic surgery (such as prostate, colon, or bladder surgery) or radiation therapy.

9
Conditions affecting the penis, such as Peyronie’s disease (curvature of the penis) or damage to the penis’s arteries, veins, or nerves.

10
Cardiovascular disease (heart disease).

11
Restricted blood flow to the penis (often due to injury).

12
Leaky veins.

Premature ejaculation (PE) is typically not caused by physical issues, though it can sometimes be linked to neurological disorders, prostate infections, or urethritis.

A hopeless man

Psychological Causes of Sexual Dysfunction:
Psychological causes of sexual dysfunction are often linked to emotional, mental, or relational issues. Stress and anxiety are common factors. Ongoing stress from work, finances, or personal concerns can reduce libido and make it difficult to relax during intimate moments. Performance anxiety, where fear of not performing well takes over, can also interfere with sexual enjoyment.

Depression can lead to a loss of interest in activities, including sex. It may also cause fatigue and emotional numbness, making it hard to connect with one's sexual needs. Relationship problems, such as poor communication or unresolved conflicts, can lead to a lack of emotional intimacy, affecting sexual connection.

For those with past trauma or abuse, sexual dysfunction can stem from emotional scars, making intimacy difficult or triggering. Negative body image can also play a role, as feeling self-conscious about one's appearance can decrease sexual confidence. Feelings of guilt or shame related to sex, often influenced by cultural or religious beliefs, can make intimacy feel uncomfortable or wrong.

Addressing these issues usually requires professional support, like counseling or therapy, and open communication with a partner. With the right help, many can overcome these challenges and improve their sexual well-being.

Can Medications Cause Sexual Problems?
Many medications can be linked to sexual dysfunction, including reduced libido and erectile dysfunction, such as:

1
High blood pressure medications

2
Diuretics (including thiazides and spironolactone)

3
Antihistamines

4
Antidepressants

5
Common over-the-counter drugs (especially antihistamines and decongestants)

6
Antipsychotic drugs

7
Sedatives

8
Anxiety medications

9
Drug use, including alcohol, methadone, heroin, anabolic steroids, and tobacco

Sexual Transmitted Diseases
Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) in males can affect the reproductive and urinary systems and lead to serious complications if left untreated. Common STDs in men include chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, and genital herpes. Symptoms can vary, but may include painful urination, unusual discharge from the penis, sores or blisters on the genital area, and itching or swelling. Some STDs, like HIV or human papillomavirus (HPV), may not show symptoms but can still be transmitted and cause long-term health issues.

The key to preventing STDs is practicing safe sex. Using condoms consistently and correctly during vaginal, anal, or oral sex reduces the risk of transmission significantly. Regular testing is essential, especially for individuals with multiple partners or those who do not consistently use protection. It's important for both partners to communicate openly about their sexual health and get tested regularly. Early detection and treatment are crucial in preventing complications, such as infertility or passing STDs to others. Safe sex not only helps protect physical health but also fosters mutual trust and respect between partners.

Environmental Factors in Sexual Problems
Enjoying a fulfilling sex life may be difficult if:

You lack a safe and private space to relax and engage in intimacy.

You are too exhausted due to work or personal commitments.

Parents may struggle to find time for intimacy due to childcare demands.

Fear of HIV/AIDS, struggles with safe sex, and the psychological effects of discrimination can also contribute to sexual anxiety in men.

Many women experience sexual dysfunction at some point in their lives, while some struggle with it throughout their lifetime. Female sexual dysfunction can occur at any stage of life and in specific sexual situations or all sexual encounters. Sexual response involves a complex interaction of physiology, emotions, experiences, beliefs, lifestyle, and relationships. A disruption in any of these components can affect desire, arousal, or sexual satisfaction, and treatment often involves multiple approaches. Persistent or recurring issues related to sexual response, desire, orgasm, or pain, causing distress or strain in a relationship are referred to as sexual dysfunction.

What is Sexual Dysfunction?
Sexual dysfunction refers to a group of conditions that can prevent an individual from engaging in or enjoying sex. These conditions can affect any stage of sexual activity, from a person’s desire to their ability to achieve orgasm. Sexual dysfunction is very common in both men and women. A 2018 study estimated a global prevalence rate of 41% among women of reproductive age. In women, sexual dysfunction can lead to difficulties with:

Desire
Low sexual desire can be classified as sexual dysfunction if it causes distress. Individuals identifying as asexual or bisexual are not included in this category, as their sexual orientation is not a medical condition.

Arousal
A person may want to have sex, but their body and mind struggle to prepare for it. For example, the vagina may not lubricate or swell as expected.

Pain
Certain conditions cause pain in or around the genitals, making sexual activity difficult. This pain may occur only during intercourse or at other times.

Orgasm
A person may engage in sex but find it difficult to reach orgasm even if they enjoy the experience.

The clinical definition of female sexual dysfunction and the disorders under this umbrella term have evolved over time. As experts gain a better understanding of female desire and arousal, this definition may continue to change.

Female Sexual Problems

What Causes Sexual Dysfunction in Women?
Contributing Factors
Physical, psychological, and social factors can all contribute to sexual dysfunction in women. The severity can be mild or severe, short-term or long-term.Some types of sexual dysfunction are primary (always present), while others are secondary (develop later due to external circumstances). For example, certain medications or medical conditions can cause secondary sexual dysfunction.In some cases, a single cause is responsible, while in others, multiple contributing factors exist.

Risk Factors
A 2018 systematic review of 135 previous studies from diverse cultures identified several risk factors associated with higher rates of sexual dysfunction, including:

Education level
Lower education levels, including limited access to general and sex education, were linked to a higher risk of sexual dysfunction.

Relationship issues
Relationship dissatisfaction, such as infidelity or lack of affection, increases the likelihood of sexual dysfunction.

Male-centered sexual interactions
A focus on male pleasure may mean that while people understand what makes sex pleasurable for men, many lack knowledge about what makes it enjoyable for women.

Health conditions
Poor physical health and diseases affecting the genitals and urinary tract are potential causes. Stress and mental health also play significant roles.

Marriage customs
Child marriage, arranged marriages, and polygamous relationships were associated with a higher risk of sexual dysfunction in women.

Religion
Studies found that religious affiliation correlated with higher levels of sexual dysfunction.

Abuse
This includes domestic abuse, sexual assault, and female genital mutilation (FGM).

Gender inequality
This global issue makes it harder for women to access sexual health services, particularly if they are unmarried and live in societies where premarital sex is stigmatized. Gender inequality also contributes to other risk factors such as abuse and FGM.

Desire and Arousal
Many factors can influence a person’s level of desire and arousal, and these often fluctuate throughout life. Some individuals naturally have a lower interest in sex than others. However, a sudden change in desire or arousal may indicate an underlying condition. Female Sexual Interest/Arousal Disorder (FSIAD) is a diagnosis that includes both lack of sexual desire and difficulty with physical arousal. To be diagnosed, a person must experience significantly reduced desire or arousal for at least six months. Someone with FSIAD may have little or no interest in sex and experience reduced pleasure during sexual activity. However, it is only classified as FSIAD if the individual feels distressed by these symptoms and no other condition better explains them, such as:

Domestic abuse

Mental illness

Medication side effects

Persistent Genital Arousal Disorder (PGAD)
PGAD causes unexplained physical sexual arousal, regardless of whether the person feels desire or wants to be aroused. The individual may even experience spontaneous orgasms. For years, doctors considered this a psychological issue. However, newer research suggests that neurological problems such as nerve damage or brain injury may be the root cause.

Pain During Sex
Pain during sex (dyspareunia) is discomfort that occurs before, during, or after intercourse. Several conditions can cause this, including:

Vaginismus: Involuntary contractions of vaginal and pelvic floor muscles before penetration, making sex painful or impossible. It may stem from trauma, anxiety, or shame related to sex.

Infections: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and yeast infections can cause pain both during and outside of sexual activity.

Skin conditions: Diseases affecting the vulva, vagina, and surrounding tissues (e.g., psoriasis, contact dermatitis) can make intercourse painful.

Endometriosis: A condition where uterine tissue grows outside the uterus, leading to pelvic adhesions and pain during sex.

Low estrogen levels: This can result in poor lubrication and thinning of vaginal tissues, causing discomfort. Estrogen levels can drop due to menopause, childbirth, or other factors.

Pelvic organ prolapse: Weakness in the pelvic floor can cause the bladder or uterus to descend into the vagina, sometimes leading to painful sex.

Pelvic floor dysfunction: Issues with pelvic muscles—such as injury, tension, or post-surgical complications—can make intercourse painful.

Orgasm
Difficulty reaching orgasm isn’t always a medical issue. Some females require more stimulation than others to climax. Exploring different techniques and communication with a partner may help. However, in some cases, Female Orgasmic Disorder (FOD) may be present. FOD is when a person:

1
Cannot reach orgasm despite adequate stimulation, or

2
Experiences a significant decrease in orgasm intensity or frequency.

FOD has two subtypes:

Primary FOD
The individual has never had an orgasm.

Secondary FOD
The person previously had orgasms but now struggles to reach them.

As with other forms of female sexual dysfunction, hormonal changes, relationship issues, and medical conditions can all contribute to FOD.

A hopeless girl

Diagnosis
Because sexual dysfunction varies widely, multiple tests may be required for an accurate diagnosis. A doctor will begin with questions about symptoms, their onset, and whether any factors improve or worsen them. They may ask about sexual history and any previous attempts to resolve the issue. Diagnostic tests may include:

Pelvic exams

STI testing

Medical imaging

Hormone testing

Mental health evaluations

content:
Sex therapy can help individuals identify and overcome sexual obstacles such as low libido, pain during intercourse, or difficulty achieving orgasm. It also aims to improve overall sexual satisfaction. This therapy is particularly beneficial for couples dealing with issues like low desire, pain during sex, difficulty reaching orgasm, and other sexual concerns. Sex therapy is a form of counseling designed to assist individuals or couples experiencing sexual difficulties. These challenges may stem from physical, psychological, or emotional factors that hinder a fulfilling sexual life. The goal is to identify the causes of these difficulties and work towards improving sexual well-being. Sex therapy can be conducted individually or with a partner, including couples therapy. It often involves both partners attending sessions together to foster open communication and improve satisfaction. However, sometimes a combination of individual and couples therapy may be recommended.

How Does It Work?
Like other forms of therapy, sex therapy involves conversations to uncover and address the root issues. This includes: 

1
Clients discuss their experiences, emotions, and concerns affecting their sexual satisfaction.

2
Therapists may suggest methods to enhance their sexual lives.

3
A therapist often assigns homework tasks like suggesting new experiences for couples to explore together.

4
If a physical issue is suspected, the therapist may refer the client to a specialist for evaluation.

Benefits of Sex Therapy
Sex therapists can assist individuals and couples by:

1
Enhancing sexual knowledge and understanding.

2
Identifying the causes of sexual difficulties.

3
Improving communication between couples.

4
Providing tailored solutions to address concerns.

5
Increasing sexual knowledge.

Who Needs Sex Therapy?
Sex therapy is recommended for individuals experiencing:

1
Premature ejaculation.

2
Erectile dysfunction.

3
Female orgasmic disorder.

4
Pain during intercourse.

5
Reduced sexual desire in men or women.

6
Sexual dysfunction caused by medication or other factors.

Sex theraphy, is just normal theraphy.

Sexual Trauma and Therapy
Sexual trauma can deeply impact desire and the ability to enjoy a healthy sexual life. Research suggests that combining trauma treatment with sex therapy is effective in helping individuals overcome past trauma and improve their sexual well-being.

The Role of Therapists
Sex therapists aim to create a comfortable environment for open discussion. Compatibility with the therapist is essential for effective treatment. They may ask questions related to:

Health and sexual knowledge.

Context and beliefs about sex.

Specific sexual difficulties.

Therapists Should Not:

Take sides or pressure clients into actions.

Remove clothing or involve clients in sexual activity.

Therapeutic Approaches
Sex therapy uses various methods tailored to the client’s needs, such as:

Problem-Solving Techniques
Improve communication between partners.

Cognitive or Behavioral Therapy
Address anxious or uncomfortable thoughts about sexual activity.

Behavioral Training
Teach clients to express sexual needs confidently.

Helpful Tips for Couples

The Start-Stop Method: Stimulate the penis until near orgasm, then pause to control excitement.

General Tips for Improving Sexual Life:

Focus on foreplay (hugging, kissing, emotional sharing).

Experiment with new experiences (e.g., toys, locations).

Reduce anxiety and stress.

Quit smoking and limit alcohol consumption.

Communicate openly (share desires and fantasies).

Exercise regularly.

Try yoga for relaxation (especially beneficial for women).

After this course, a follow-up course is offered for those who want to learn more about the topic or pursue a career as a sex coach.

title: LGBTQ+

content:
LGBTQ stands for lesbian, gay, bisexual, or individuals whose sexual orientation is undetermined. Sexual orientation refers to a person's romantic or sexual attraction to others, which can emerge at a young age, often without sexual desires being involved. It becomes stronger and more defined as a person matures and shapes their sexual identity. Sexual orientation can be fluid for some people, while for others, it remains fixed. Importantly, it is not a choice and cannot be changed through therapy or external influence. For example, a little girl preferring toys typically associated with boys does not necessarily indicate she is lesbian. Recognizing someone’s sexual orientation may be straightforward in some cases but challenging in others. For instance, a girl attracted to both boys and girls is likely bisexual. However, some individuals take years to understand their orientation, with many referring to themselves as "questioning" during this process, especially during adolescence.

LGBTQ+ and mental health
​LGBTQ+ individuals often face significant mental health challenges, with studies highlighting notably higher rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts compared to their heterosexual and cisgender peers. A comprehensive analysis of the 2022 National Health Interview Survey revealed that approximately 49% of sexual minorities experienced depression, and 44.3% dealt with anxiety, in contrast to 19.5% and 16.4% respectively among heterosexual individuals. ​

Social rejection and lack of acceptance can be particularly harmful. LGBTQ+ individuals may experience family rejection, bullying at school, or discrimination in the workplace, all of which can severely impact their mental well-being. Many LGBTQ+ youth, for instance, experience homelessness or are forced to live in unsafe environments because their families do not accept their identity. Additionally, internalized homophobia or transphobia can occur, where individuals internalize negative societal attitudes about LGBTQ+ people, leading to feelings of guilt, shame, and depression. This internalized stigma can make it harder for people to accept themselves, further exacerbating mental health issues.

For transgender individuals, gender dysphoria,the distress caused by a mismatch between one’s gender identity and assigned sex at birth, can also contribute to mental health challenges, such as depression and anxiety. Transgender people often face additional barriers to accessing healthcare, including gender-affirming care, which can increase stress and anxiety.

Furthermore, the lack of supportive mental health services and professionals trained in LGBTQ+ issues can make it harder for individuals to find appropriate care. The compounded stress from societal challenges, coupled with inadequate mental health support, contributes to higher rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation in the LGBTQ+ community.

The Difference Between Sex and Gender
It’s essential to distinguish biological sex from gender and sexual orientation. These concepts are related but distinct:

Biological Sex
Determined at birth based on genitalia, biological sex is recorded as male or female. Some individuals do not fit neatly into these categories and may identify as non-binary.

Gender (Social Perspective)
Societal norms dictate how individuals are expected to dress, behave, or think based on being male or female. These cultural expectations vary widely, such as men being encouraged to display anger in some societies.

Gender Identity
Refers to how individuals perceive themselves and express their identity through clothing, behavior, and appearance. Some people may identify as neither strictly male nor female, often referring to themselves as genderqueer.

What Does "Coming Out" Mean?
Coming out refers to the process of realizing and sharing one's sexual orientation or gender identity with others. Every individual has their own way of coming out, and for some, it may be a private acknowledgment of their identity. Coming out is a deeply personal decision. It can be a significant milestone but should only occur when the individual feels ready and safe. For many, it is a recurring process throughout life as they meet new people and navigate various situations.

Gender Transition in Vietnam

A transgender, who looks girly.

A study by a transgender organization in the Asia-Pacific region revealed that transgender individuals typically recognize their gender identity between the ages of 12 and 14, with the average age for coming out being 17. However, the process often involves significant stress, insomnia, and anxiety, with many experiencing suicidal thoughts.

In Vietnam, the lack of official regulations on hormone therapy and gender reassignment surgery poses challenges. Many transgender individuals resort to self-administering hormones, which can be harmful. Statistics show nearly 73% of transgender people purchase hormones illegally. Furthermore, transgender individuals frequently face bullying, sexual abuse, and employment discrimination, with many being rejected by companies based solely on their resumes.

Same-Sex Marriage in Vietnam
Although same-sex marriage is not legally recognized in Vietnam, progress has been made. In 2013, the government announced that same-sex weddings would not be penalized, but they remain unrecognized under the law. This leaves same-sex couples without legal protections for social security, inheritance, or adoption rights. While Vietnam is relatively open about homosexuality compared to some countries, there is no national data on same-sex marriages, unlike other South Asian nations where the rate ranges from 4% to 10%.

A Personal Story
I consider myself a 100% straight boy, but I’ve always been open-minded toward the LGBTQ+ community. My personal philosophy is simple: do whatever you want, as long as you don’t harm others. Live and let live. With that mindset, I’ve spent a lot of weekends visiting different cities around Asia, exploring new cultures and meeting new people. A few years ago, I was in Hanoi, the capital of Vietnam, when I met a ladyboy. We sat down for a drink, had a great conversation, and quickly became friends. Our friendship was based on enjoying each other’s company and having meaningful talks, not on any sexual activities. I always respected her as a person, and she identified as a woman, so I referred to her as “she” out of respect.

Over the years, I would visit her once or twice a year when I came to Hanoi. Our meetups typically consisted of sitting next to the large lake, having a barbecue, sharing cigarettes, and enjoying a bottle of wine. During these moments, she often shared with me the struggles of her life—financial hardships, being abandoned by her family, enduring bullying during her teenage years, and the constant risk of contracting an STD because of her work, which involved "selling her body" as she put it. We’d spend hours just talking, walking through the streets, sitting in coffee bars, or hanging out by the lake, and I never cared what others thought of us. It was always a genuine connection, and I never imagined how hard her life truly was. She seemed so strong, yet I could tell she carried a lot of pain.

Then, about two years ago, I tried reaching out to her again. I was planning another visit to Hanoi and invited her for a coffee. But I never got a response. I tried a few more times, but she didn’t read her messages. I called her, sent texts, and even went to her house in Hanoi, but she was gone. The neighbors didn’t know where she had gone either. It was as though she had vanished. The last conversation I remember clearly is when she told me that one day, she would go to Thailand to find a lover and start a new life, leaving everything behind. She said she wanted to forget her past. I’ve always hoped that’s the reason why I never heard from her again—that she found the peace she was looking for, somewhere far away from her past.

I still think of her sometimes and wonder where she might be. Our friendship taught me a lot about resilience, acceptance, and the struggles people face that others may never see. I hope she’s out there living the life she dreamed of.

For many, it is a recurring process throughout life as they meet new people and navigate various situations.

Gender Transition in Vietnam

A transgender, who looks girly.

A study by a transgender organization in the Asia-Pacific region revealed that transgender individuals typically recognize their gender identity between the ages of 12 and 14, with the average age for coming out being 17. However, the process often involves significant stress, insomnia, and anxiety, with many experiencing suicidal thoughts.

In Vietnam, the lack of official regulations on hormone therapy and gender reassignment surgery poses challenges. Many transgender individuals resort to self-administering hormones, which can be harmful. Statistics show nearly 73% of transgender people purchase hormones illegally. Furthermore, transgender individuals frequently face bullying, sexual abuse, and employment discrimination, with many being rejected by companies based solely on their resumes.

Same-Sex Marriage in Vietnam

Although same-sex marriage is not legally recognized in Vietnam, progress has been made. In 2013, the government announced that same-sex weddings would not be penalized, but they remain unrecognized under the law. This leaves same-sex couples without legal protections for social security, inheritance, or adoption rights. While Vietnam is relatively open about homosexuality compared to some countries, there is no national data on same-sex marriages, unlike other South Asian nations where the rate ranges from 4% to 10%.

A Personal Story

I consider myself a 100% straight boy, but I’ve always been open-minded toward the LGBTQ+ community. My personal philosophy is simple: do whatever you want, as long as you don’t harm others. Live and let live. With that mindset, I’ve spent a lot of weekends visiting different cities around Asia, exploring new cultures and meeting new people. A few years ago, I was in Hanoi, the capital of Vietnam, when I met a ladyboy. We sat down for a drink, had a great conversation, and quickly became friends. Our friendship was based on enjoying each other’s company and having meaningful talks, not on any sexual activities. I always respected her as a person, and she identified as a woman, so I referred to her as “she” out of respect.

Over the years, I would visit her once or twice a year when I came to Hanoi. Our meetups typically consisted of sitting next to the large lake, having a barbecue, sharing cigarettes, and enjoying a bottle of wine. During these moments, she often shared with me the struggles of her life—financial hardships, being abandoned by her family, enduring bullying during her teenage years, and the constant risk of contracting an STD because of her work, which involved "selling her body" as she put it. We’d spend hours just talking, walking through the streets, sitting in coffee bars, or hanging out by the lake, and I never cared what others thought of us. It was always a genuine connection, and I never imagined how hard her life truly was. She seemed so strong, yet I could tell she carried a lot of pain.

Then, about two years ago, I tried reaching out to her again. I was planning another visit to Hanoi and invited her for a coffee. But I never got a response. I tried a few more times, but she didn’t read her messages. I called her, sent texts, and even went to her house in Hanoi, but she was gone. The neighbors didn’t know where she had gone either. It was as though she had vanished. The last conversation I remember clearly is when she told me that one day, she would go to Thailand to find a lover and start a new life, leaving everything behind. She said she wanted to forget her past. I’ve always hoped that’s the reason why I never heard from her again—that she found the peace she was looking for, somewhere far away from her past.

I still think of her sometimes and wonder where she might be. Our friendship taught me a lot about resilience, acceptance, and the struggles people face that others may never see. I hope she’s out there living the life she dreamed of.

content:
An unhealthy relationship is one where one or both individuals experience negative patterns of behavior that can harm their emotional, mental, or physical well-being. These relationships may involve manipulation, control, or a lack of mutual respect. Below are some key characteristics of unhealthy relationships:

Lack of Respect: One person consistently disregards the other’s feelings, boundaries, or needs. Disrespect can also appear as belittling, name-calling, or constant criticism.

Control and Manipulation: One partner may try to control or manipulate the other’s actions, decisions, or relationships with others. This can include isolating the partner from friends or family, monitoring their movements, or trying to control their behavior.

Constant Conflict or Drama: There is a persistent cycle of fighting, arguments, or emotional turmoil that never seems to resolve. This can create a toxic environment where both individuals feel drained or unsafe.

Lack of Communication: Healthy communication is key in any relationship. In an unhealthy relationship, communication is either non-existent, passive-aggressive, or one-sided, where one person dominates the conversation while the other is silenced or ignored.

Emotional or Physical Abuse: This can range from verbal abuse (e.g., insults, threats) to physical violence. Abuse in any form is a clear indicator of an unhealthy relationship and can have long-term impacts on a person's mental and physical health.

Dishonesty: Lying, cheating, or withholding important information can erode trust and lead to feelings of betrayal. Trust is a fundamental aspect of a healthy relationship, and when it's broken, the relationship becomes unhealthy.

Lack of Support: In an unhealthy relationship, one partner may fail to support the other emotionally, mentally, or physically. Instead of building each other up, one person may drain the other or remain indifferent to their struggles.

Unequal Power Dynamics: An unhealthy relationship often involves one person having more power or control over the other, leading to an imbalance. This could be through financial control, emotional manipulation, or making all the decisions without considering the other person's input.

In unhealthy relationships, both individuals may feel unfulfilled, unsafe, or unhappy. It's important to recognize these signs early and seek help or support to either address the issues or, in some cases, end the relationship for the well-being of everyone involved.

Relationship problems

The Roots of Stable Relationships
Love is one of the deepest and most profound emotions in human life. While there are many kinds of love, it is often described in terms of romantic relationships. For many people, romantic connections are a source of inspiration and fulfillment. The need for connection is inherent in humans, but maintaining a healthy romantic relationship requires skills that are developed over time. Research suggests that the foundation of stable relationships begins in childhood, during interactions with parents or caregivers. When children experience care, warmth, and protection, they develop an understanding of relationships. These early experienceswhere basic needs like food, care, and safety are met, create patterns that shape an individual’s approach to relationships. While these early patterns influence relationships, they are not fixed and can evolve with effort and experience.

Building a Healthy Relationship
Healthy relationships are built on mutual care, trust, and effective communication. Regardless of the type of relationship, certain core characteristics help determine its health and stability. Key aspects of a strong relationship include:

Mutual Commitment
Both partners should feel confident that the other is willing to invest time and effort into the relationship.

Teamwork
Both partners must work together to navigate life’s challenges.

Balance
A good relationship includes emotional and physical balance. This could mean sharing household responsibilities, expressing gratitude, and openly discussing feelings and needs.

A heart. the sign of love.

Tips for Building and Maintaining a Strong Relationship
Here are practical ways to strengthen your relationship and address challenges:

Prioritize Communication
Set aside regular time to talk about your relationship and spend quality time together.

Be Honest
Share your true feelings with each other.

Resolve Recurring Issues
Identify common problems and work collaboratively to find solutions.

Work as a Team
Understand that your partner may not fulfill every role but can be a valuable teammate.

Find Shared Interests
Explore hobbies, activities, or sports that both of you enjoy.

Discuss Finances
Have open and honest conversations about money matters.

Show Love Daily
Small gestures of love and appreciation can strengthen the bond.

Engage in Positive Dialogue
Approach discussions with positivity and aim for mutual agreements.

Seek Support
Turn to friends or professionals for advice when needed.
