content:
Case Study: Minh and the Daily Struggles of Autism

Minh is a 12-year-old boy living in Ho Chi Minh City with his parents and 7-year-old sister, An. He was diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) when he was five years old. Minh is a bright child with an extraordinary memory, he can recall the dates of family events, recite entire passages from his favorite books, and even memorize bus routes around the city.

Despite his intelligence, Minh struggles with many aspects of daily life. His parents first noticed something unusual when he was three. While other children were talking and playing with each other, Minh preferred lining up his toy cars for hours or staring at the rotating fan in fascination. He rarely made eye contact and often seemed lost in his own world. As he grew older, the challenges became more apparent:

School Life:
Minh attends a public school, but every day is a battle. Group activities make him uncomfortable, and he often avoids speaking to classmates. He rarely understands sarcasm or jokes, which makes socializing difficult. His teacher notices that while he excels in math, he struggles to follow instructions in subjects that require writing essays or teamwork.

Sensory Sensitivities:
Noise is Minh’s greatest enemy. The sound of the school bell makes him cover his ears and sometimes cry. Even a crowded market near his house can trigger panic. His parents have to carefully plan outings to avoid overwhelming environments.

Home Challenges:
Simple tasks like getting ready for school can take a long time. Minh dislikes the feeling of certain fabrics on his skin, so choosing clothes becomes a struggle. He needs multiple reminders to brush his teeth, and changes in routine, like a sudden trip to visit relatives, can lead to meltdowns.

Minh’s parents love him deeply, but raising him is emotionally exhausting. His mother, Lan, often worries about his future:

“Will he be able to live independently one day? Will people understand and accept him?”

His father, Huy, sometimes feels frustrated when Minh refuses to try new things or shuts down during family gatherings. An, his little sister, is cheerful and loving, but she sometimes feels left out when most attention goes to Minh.

In the last year, Minh has become more withdrawn. He spends hours in his room reading or arranging his collections of stones and bottle caps. He avoids family meals and becomes visibly anxious if his parents suggest he join a school activity. Recently, his teacher informed his parents that Minh had a meltdown in class after a sudden change in schedule, and he refused to come to school for two days.

The family feels trapped and overwhelmed, unsure how to help Minh navigate the world while also caring for their own emotional needs.

How a Life Coach Can Support Minh and His Family

A life coach who understands neurodiversity can offer practical guidance, emotional support, and strategies that make daily life more manageable for the entire family.

Creating a Safe, Supportive Environment

The coach begins by building trust with Minh, allowing him to express himself through his interests instead of forcing verbal communication.

They also help the parents acknowledge and accept Minh’s pace of development, focusing on strengths rather than only challenges.

Building Routines and Predictability

Autistic children thrive on structure. The coach can help design clear, visual schedules for Minh’s mornings, homework, and bedtime.

This reduces anxiety, as Minh knows what to expect each day. Even small routines like a visual checklist for getting dressed can prevent morning meltdowns.

Developing Emotional and Social Skills

Through role-playing games, storytelling, or visual emotion charts, the coach helps Minh identify and express feelings like “happy,” “sad,” “angry,” and “scared.”

They gradually practice simple social interactions, like greeting a classmate or asking for help, building his confidence over time.

Managing Sensory Overload

The coach can introduce coping tools such as noise-canceling headphones, quiet spaces at home, or calming techniques like deep breathing and fidget toys.

Minh learns to recognize the early signs of sensory overload and use these tools before reaching a meltdown.

Parental Guidance and Family Balance

Life coaching sessions also focus on helping Lan and Huy manage stress and avoid burnout.

The coach encourages the family to celebrate small wins, such as Minh trying a new food or participating in a short group activity.

They also ensure that little An receives attention and emotional support, fostering a healthier family dynamic.

Goal Setting and Positive Reinforcement

Together, the coach and family set achievable goals for Minh, such as:

Getting dressed independently three times a week

Attending a school activity for 30 minutes

Joining a family meal without leaving early

Celebrating these milestones helps Minh feel proud and motivates him to take the next step.

With the guidance of a life coach, Minh’s family can shift from a cycle of stress and uncertainty to one of structure, hope, and gradual progress. Minh may continue to face challenges, but with patience, consistent support, and a focus on his unique strengths, he can gain the skills and confidence to navigate his world more successfully, and his family can regain balance and peace at home.

Career opportunities for coaches with expertise in ADHD are very promising in Vietnam. This is because there is a shortage of coaches who are knowledgeable about the disorder. Coaches can work with families, children, and individuals, offering support in various areas. One of the key areas a coach can assist with is improving planning and organization skills, which are essential for managing ADHD effectively.

Key Points
ADHD is a neurological disorder that affects attention, impulse control, and hyperactivity. It impacts both children and adults, with symptoms varying in severity.

ADHD in women is often underdiagnosed because symptoms can be more internalized, such as inattention and disorganization. Hormonal changes can also influence the severity of symptoms.

ADHD is diagnosed through a comprehensive evaluation, which includes behavioral assessments and consideration of co-occurring conditions like anxiety or depression.

Common treatments for ADHD include behavioral therapy, ADHD coaching, medication (stimulants or non-stimulants), and lifestyle changes such as exercise and structured routines.

ADHD can affect academic, professional, and personal life, with individuals often facing challenges in organization, time management, and emotional regulation.

Approximately 3–8% of children in Vietnam have ADHD, making learning and daily activities challenging. Adults with ADHD also face significant difficulties in their lives. There are three main types of ADHD, and understanding which type a patient has is crucial for appropriate treatment.

content:
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental condition that affects both children and adults. It is characterized by symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. While ADHD is most commonly diagnosed in childhood, many individuals continue to experience symptoms into adulthood, often impacting various aspects of their personal, academic, and professional lives.

Approximately 8.4% of children and 2.5% of adults are estimated to have ADHD.

ADHD is often identified in school-aged children when it disrupts classroom activities or learning.

It is diagnosed more frequently in boys due to differences in symptom presentation.

Diagnosis and Assessment
ADHD is diagnosed based on behavioral symptoms observed over a long period of time (at least six months). A comprehensive evaluation typically includes interviews, behavioral checklists, and input from parents, teachers, or partners. For adults, the diagnosis may involve a thorough history of childhood behavior and current symptoms. It is essential to rule out other conditions that may mimic ADHD, such as anxiety or learning disabilities.

ADHD in Adults
For adults with ADHD, the challenges continue into the workplace and personal life. Adults may find it difficult to stay organized, meet deadlines, and manage responsibilities. This can hinder career progression and contribute to stress, frustration, and a diminished sense of self-worth. They may also experience heightened sensitivity to criticism, stemming from years of being negatively judged for behaviors linked to ADHD.

Symptoms of ADHD in Adults

Inattention
Adults with ADHD often struggle to focus, stay organized, and follow through on tasks. They are frequently forgetful, misplacing items like keys or paperwork, which can make daily activities feel overwhelming.

Impulsivity
Adults with ADHD can include making hasty decisions, interrupting others during conversations, or difficulty waiting for turns. These actions can lead to conflicts in relationships or at work. Additionally, impulsivity may result in risky behaviors like reckless driving, overspending, or substance use, which can have serious consequences.

Restlessness
While hyperactivity may decrease with age, adults with ADHD often experience restlessness, feeling the need to constantly move or fidget. They may also find it hard to relax or sit still for extended periods. Additionally, sleep problems, such as difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up too early, are common, which can further exacerbate restlessness and affect overall well-being.

Disorganization
Difficulty organizing tasks and managing time is common, which can lead to missed deadlines, appointments, or responsibilities.

ADHD in Adults

ADHD in Children
ADHD is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders diagnosed in childhood. It affects a child's ability to focus, control impulses, and regulate their activity level, impacting various aspects of their academic and social life. Though symptoms can continue into adulthood, early diagnosis and intervention are crucial to help children manage their symptoms and thrive. Many children with ADHD show a reduction in symptoms as they transition into adulthood. While the core characteristics of ADHD may still be present, they often become less intense and more manageable over time. This does not mean the disorder disappears, but rather that individuals may develop coping strategies and the symptoms may present differently in adulthood.

Core Symptoms of ADHD in Children
Inattention: Children with ADHD often struggle to focus on tasks, especially those that require sustained attention, like homework or listening to lessons. They may be easily distracted by external stimuli, forget instructions, or have difficulty following through on tasks.

Hyperactivity: Children with ADHD may show excessive physical movement, such as running, fidgeting, or being unable to sit still when expected. This hyperactivity can be especially noticeable in structured settings like classrooms.

Impulsivity: Impulsivity in children with ADHD may involve interrupting others, difficulty waiting for their turn, or making hasty decisions without considering consequences. This can lead to challenges in social interactions and academic settings.

Signs in children

Impact on a Child’s Daily Life
One of the most significant struggles is social difficulties. Due to impulsivity or trouble understanding social cues, many children with ADHD become targets for bullying, which can lead to social isolation and a negative impact on their self-esteem. This sense of being different can stick with them into adulthood, affecting their ability to form lasting relationships.

Another common issue is sleep disturbances. Many children and adults with ADHD struggle with falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up too early. These sleep issues can exacerbate other symptoms of ADHD, such as irritability, lack of focus, and mood swings. When sleep is disrupted, it becomes even harder to manage the day-to-day challenges of ADHD.

Academically, children with ADHD often struggle to stay on task. They may have difficulty organizing their schoolwork, completing assignments on time, or following instructions in the classroom. They may also forget important tasks or lose their belongings frequently, such as textbooks, homework, or personal items. This often leads to frustration, poor grades, and feelings of failure. As they grow older, these difficulties can persist in the workplace, making time management and meeting deadlines a constant challenge. Impulsivity can also carry over into adulthood, where individuals may make hasty decisions that lead to financial problems, reckless driving, or risky behaviors like substance use.

The emotional toll of ADHD can also be significant. Constant struggles with attention, behavior, and performance can chip away at self-esteem, leading to anxiety and depression. These mental health challenges can make it even harder to manage ADHD symptoms and build a positive outlook on life. Additionally, many people with ADHD struggle with emotional regulation, leading to outbursts or difficulty dealing with stress in both personal and professional relationships.

Finally, it’s common for ADHD to co-occur with other conditions like learning disabilities, anxiety, or depression. These overlapping issues can complicate diagnosis and treatment, making it harder to address all the factors contributing to a person’s struggles. Overall, ADHD can have a profound effect on many aspects of life, but with early intervention, support, and effective treatment strategies, individuals can learn to manage their symptoms and thrive in their personal and professional lives.

Treatment and Management of ADHD

Medication
Stimulant medications, such as methylphenidate (Ritalin) or amphetamines (Adderall), are commonly prescribed to children with ADHD to help improve focus, impulse control, and reduce hyperactivity. Non-stimulant medications, like atomoxetine (Strattera), may be used if children do not respond well to stimulants.

Behavioral Therapy
Behavioral interventions, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), focus on teaching children coping strategies, self-regulation techniques, and how to improve organizational skills. Parent training is often part of therapy to help manage behavior at home.

Educational Support
Children with ADHD may benefit from accommodations in school, such as extended time for tests, a quiet space to complete assignments, or additional support from a special education teacher. Creating a structured learning environment can help these children stay on track and succeed academically.

Parent and Teacher Collaboration
Effective treatment often involves close collaboration between parents, teachers, and healthcare providers to ensure that a child’s needs are met across different environments. Consistency in rules, routines, and rewards can help children with ADHD thrive.

ADHD Coaching
ADHD coaching focuses on improving organizational skills, setting goals, and creating strategies to manage daily tasks and responsibilities. Coaches work one-on-one with individuals to help them achieve their personal and professional goals.

A toy can be very useful for children with ADHD to stay forcused in class.

A positive message about ADHD
ADHD is often associated with unique strengths and abilities that can lead to great achievements. Many people with ADHD possess exceptional creativity and artistic talent. For example, there are numerous renowned musicians, dancers, and visual artists who have ADHD, as their hyperactive and energetic nature often translates into powerful, expressive performances. Their ability to think outside the box and approach problems from unconventional angles can lead to groundbreaking ideas and innovations.

Additionally, people with ADHD are often very sensitive and empathetic. This sensitivity allows them to form deep connections with others, and they are frequently drawn to animals, as they can relate to their emotions. This connection often results in a strong bond with pets, offering both comfort and companionship.

People with ADHD are also known for their enthusiasm and passion. When they find something they are interested in, they can dive in wholeheartedly and pour energy and focus into it, leading to remarkable achievements in their chosen fields. Their ability to think quickly and make decisions under pressure is another strength, especially in fast-paced environments or creative industries.

Ultimately, while ADHD may present challenges, it also brings a wealth of potential that can shine brightly in many aspects of life, from artistic expression to building meaningful relationships.

title: ADHD in Women
about: ADHD in girls is often underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed, as their symptoms can be more subtle compared to boys. While boys with ADHD tend to display hyperactive and impulsive behaviors, girls are more likely to show symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty focusing, forgetfulnes
content:
ADHD in girls is often underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed, as their symptoms can be more subtle compared to boys. While boys with ADHD tend to display hyperactive and impulsive behaviors, girls are more likely to show symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty focusing, forgetfulness, and disorganization. These traits can be overlooked or mistaken for other issues, such as anxiety or depression.

Girls with ADHD may struggle with staying on task, following through on assignments, or keeping track of their belongings. They can be more prone to daydreaming and may have trouble with time management and planning. Social difficulties can also arise, as girls may find it hard to read social cues or maintain conversations, leading to feelings of isolation or low self-esteem.

Hormonal changes, such as those during puberty, menstruation, or pregnancy, can also affect ADHD symptoms, making them more pronounced or harder to manage. Girls may experience mood swings or increased emotional sensitivity during these times, which can complicate the diagnosis and treatment of ADHD. It’s important for parents, teachers, and healthcare professionals to be aware of how ADHD presents in girls so that they can receive the appropriate support and treatment. Early diagnosis and intervention can help girls with ADHD manage their symptoms, build confidence, and succeed academically and socially.

ADHD in Girls

The Complexity of Diagnosing ADHD in Women
Diagnosing ADHD in women presents unique challenges:

Bias in Childhood: Teachers and parents may overlook ADHD symptoms in girls due to unconscious biases, making referrals for evaluation less common.

Subtle Symptoms: Women often show "hidden" symptoms, such as inattention, which can be easily misdiagnosed or go untreated.

Inattentiveness vs. Hyperactivity: Women are more likely to exhibit inattentiveness (difficulty focusing) rather than the hyperactivity seen in boys.

Coexisting Challenges
Women with ADHD may also experience:

Bias in Childhood
Teachers and parents may overlook ADHD symptoms in girls due to unconscious biases, making referrals for evaluation less common.

Subtle Symptoms
Women often show “hidden” symptoms, such as inattention, which can be easily misdiagnosed or go untreated.

Inattentiveness vs. Hyperactivity
Women are more likely to exhibit inattentiveness (difficulty focusing) rather than the hyperactivity seen in boys.

Not all women with ADHD experience these challenges, so a comprehensive evaluation is crucial.

Differences Between Girls and Boys
Symptom Presentation:

Girls: Forgetfulness, difficulty focusing, and organizational issues (inattentiveness)

Boys: Hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as blurting out or inability to sit still

Diagnosis Challenges:

Girls' symptoms are often mistaken for anxiety or depression, delaying diagnosis.

Hormonal fluctuations can cause inconsistent symptoms, further complicating diagnosis.

Without noticeable hyperactive behaviors, many girls remain undiagnosed until adolescence, often struggling with ADHD symptoms for years.

A female, trying to focus.

Seeking Support and Treatment
If you suspect you have ADHD, here are steps to take:

Consult a Doctor
A medical professional can provide an accurate diagnosis, often supplemented by neuropsychological tests.

Medications
Options include stimulants, non-stimulants, and antidepressants (off-label for ADHD).

Psychotherapy
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) helps with negative thought patterns, procrastination, and improving organizational skills.

Join a Support Group
Connect with others who share similar experiences and strategies.

Lifestyle Adjustments
Healthy habits like regular exercise, a balanced diet, and sufficient sleep can help manage symptoms.

Structured Routines
Use planning tools, break tasks into steps, and maintain a structured routine to stay organized.

Self-Care
Prioritize activities that reduce stress, such as hobbies or mindfulness practices.

title: ADD
about: ADD (Attention Deficit Disorder) is an older term that was once used to describe individuals who had difficulty with attention, focus, and organization, but did not exhibit the hyperactive or impulsive behaviors that are typically associated with ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperacti
content:
ADD (Attention Deficit Disorder) is an older term that was once used to describe individuals who had difficulty with attention, focus, and organization, but did not exhibit the hyperactive or impulsive behaviors that are typically associated with ADHD (Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder). In the past, ADD was used to identify a specific subset of individuals with attention difficulties who didn’t display the common signs of hyperactivity, such as fidgeting, impulsiveness, or excessive movement.

1. ADHD, Inattentive Type (formerly known as ADD): This type involves difficulties with attention, focus, and organization, but without the hyperactive or impulsive behaviors. Individuals with this type may struggle to stay on task, follow through on assignments, or organize their thoughts, but they typically do not engage in excessive movement or impulsive actions.

2. ADHD, Hyperactive-Impulsive Type: This type is characterized by symptoms of hyperactivity and impulsivity, such as fidgeting, difficulty sitting still, interrupting others, or acting without thinking. People with this type may have trouble controlling their impulses, leading to challenges in both social and academic situations.

3. ADHD, Combined Type: This type involves a combination of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms. Individuals with ADHD, Combined Type, exhibit symptoms of both attention-related issues and hyperactivity/impulsivity.

Key Differences:
ADD is no longer used as an official diagnosis. It is now considered a part of ADHD, specifically referring to individuals with ADHD who only experience attentional difficulties and do not exhibit hyperactivity or impulsivity.

The primary difference between ADD (now ADHD, Inattentive Type) and ADHD as a whole is the presence of hyperactivity and impulsivity. Those with ADHD, Inattentive Type may struggle with staying focused, organizing tasks, and following through on commitments but generally don’t display the restless, impulsive behaviors seen in other types of ADHD.

In summary, ADD is an outdated term for what is now called ADHD, Inattentive Type. ADHD is the umbrella term that covers all types of attention and behavior regulation challenges, including both inattentiveness and hyperactivity. The distinction now lies in the different symptoms—whether someone primarily struggles with attention or also displays hyperactivity and impulsivity.

title: Facts and Myths
about:
Myth: ADHD is just a lack of discipline.

Fact: ADHD is a neurological condition that affects brain function, making it harder for individuals to focus, organize, and control impulses.

Myth: ADHD only affects children.

Fact: ADHD continues into adulthood for many individuals, t
content:
Myth: ADHD is just a lack of discipline.

Fact: ADHD is a neurological condition that affects brain function, making it harder for individuals to focus, organize, and control impulses.

Myth: ADHD only affects children.

Fact: ADHD continues into adulthood for many individuals, though it may present differently as people age.

Myth: People with ADHD are always hyperactive.

Fact: Not everyone with ADHD is hyperactive. Many individuals primarily experience symptoms of inattention or impulsivity.

Myth: Children with ADHD will outgrow it.

Fact: While some symptoms may improve with age, many individuals continue to experience ADHD symptoms into adulthood.

Myth: ADHD is caused by bad parenting.

Fact: ADHD is a complex condition with genetic and neurological factors; it is not caused by parenting style.

Myth: Medication is the only treatment for ADHD.

Fact: While medication can be effective, other treatments such as therapy, behavioral interventions, and lifestyle changes can also help manage ADHD symptoms.

Myth: People with ADHD can’t be successful.

Fact: With proper support, people with ADHD can excel in many areas, including creative fields, leadership, and problem-solving.

Myth: ADHD is a rare condition.

Fact: ADHD is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders, affecting about 5–10% of the population worldwide.

Myth: All people with ADHD are easily distracted.

Fact: While distractibility is common, some people with ADHD may hyper-focus on certain tasks, often losing track of time or neglecting other responsibilities.

Myth: ADHD is over-diagnosed.

Fact: Many people, especially girls and adults, go undiagnosed or misdiagnosed, meaning ADHD is often under-recognized, not over-diagnosed.

Fact: Not everyone with ADHD is hyperactive. Many individuals primarily experience symptoms of inattention or impulsivity.

Myth: Children with ADHD will outgrow it.

Fact: While some symptoms may improve with age, many individuals continue to experience ADHD symptoms into adulthood.

Myth: ADHD is caused by bad parenting.

Fact: ADHD is a complex condition with genetic and neurological factors; it is not caused by parenting style.

Myth: Medication is the only treatment for ADHD.

Fact: While medication can be effective, other treatments such as therapy, behavioral interventions, and lifestyle changes can also help manage ADHD symptoms.

Myth: People with ADHD can’t be successful.

Fact: With proper support, people with ADHD can excel in many areas, including creative fields, leadership, and problem-solving.

Myth: ADHD is a rare condition.

Fact: ADHD is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders, affecting about 5–10% of the population worldwide.

Myth: All people with ADHD are easily distracted.

Fact: While distractibility is common, some people with ADHD may hyper-focus on certain tasks, often losing track of time or neglecting other responsibilities.

Myth: ADHD is over-diagnosed.

Fact: Many people, especially girls and adults, go undiagnosed or misdiagnosed, meaning ADHD is often under-recognized, not over-diagnosed.

content:
Case Study: Long and the Challenges of ADHD

Long is a 15-year-old high school student living in Hanoi with his parents and older brother. He was diagnosed with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) at age 10. Long is energetic, creative, and loves sports, but he struggles greatly with focus, organization, and impulsive behavior.

From early childhood, his parents noticed that Long was constantly moving, easily distracted, and quick to speak or act without thinking. While other children could sit quietly for storytime, Long often fidgeted, interrupted, or wandered around the classroom. In high school, his ADHD symptoms have become more challenging:

Academic Difficulties:
Long has trouble completing homework on time and often forgets to bring assignments or books to class. He understands the lessons but gets distracted after a few minutes, missing key instructions. Tests are stressful because he makes careless mistakes even when he knows the material.

Behavioral Struggles:
Long is impulsive and sometimes blurts out answers in class or interrupts teachers. His friends like his playful nature, but some find him unpredictable and hard to work with in group projects.

Emotional Impact:
Constant reminders from teachers and scolding at home make Long feel frustrated and misunderstood. He sometimes thinks he is “lazy” or “not smart enough,” which affects his self-esteem.

Home Life:
Mornings are chaotic—Long often forgets to pack his bag or leaves homework behind. Evenings are filled with arguments about screen time, chores, and unfinished assignments. His parents are loving but exhausted, unsure how to manage his energy.

Long’s parents fear that if this pattern continues, he will fall behind in school and lose motivation, while Long just feels trapped in a cycle of trying and failing.

How a Life Coach Can Support Long and His Family

Life coaching for ADHD does not replace therapy or medical treatment, but it can help children like Long develop life skills, structure, and self-confidence.

Creating Structure and Routine

The coach helps Long and his parents create a clear daily schedule with set times for schoolwork, breaks, meals, and bedtime.

Visual charts or checklists can guide Long to pack his schoolbag, complete assignments, and manage chores without constant reminders.

Improving Focus with Small Steps

The coach teaches Long to break large tasks into smaller, achievable steps.

Building Self-Awareness and Self-Esteem

Life coaching emphasizes Long’s strengths, such as his creativity and energy, rather than only focusing on his mistakes.

Celebrating small achievements, like finishing homework or staying focused for a full session, builds confidence and motivation.

Developing Organizational Skills

The coach helps Long create simple systems for school and home, such as a color-coded folder system or a homework checklist.

A dedicated, distraction-free study corner at home reinforces the habit of focusing.

Teaching Emotional Regulation

Through role-playing and short mindfulness or breathing exercises, Long learns to pause before reacting impulsively in class or at home.

The coach guides his parents in responding calmly, using positive reinforcement instead of frequent criticism.

Parental Support and Collaboration

Life coaching includes parents, teaching them how to give clear instructions, set realistic expectations, and support Long’s independence.

By working as a team, the family reduces conflict and replaces arguments with encouragement.

With the support of a life coach, Long can slowly turn his challenges into manageable tasks. By learning structure, emotional regulation, and self-confidence, he gains tools to succeed in school and daily life. At the same time, his family learns to support him with patience and consistency, creating a home environment where Long can thrive.

Career opportunities for a speech coach in Vietnam are quite promising, especially because the field is not yet well-developed and there is a growing demand for professionals. As there are fewer speech coaches available in the country, this presents a unique opportunity for those with expertise in speech and language therapy. One key area where speech professionals are in high demand is among international students, particularly those in the lower year levels. These students often face challenges in adapting to new languages, communication styles, and academic environments. A speech coach can provide invaluable support to help these students improve their language skills, pronunciation, and confidence in speaking.

Key Points
Speech Disorders: Conditions that affect speech sounds, fluency, voice, and resonance, such as stuttering, articulation issues, and voice disorders.

Types of Speech Disorders: Includes articulation disorders (difficulty pronouncing sounds), fluency disorders (stuttering), voice disorders (pitch/volume issues), and resonance disorders (nasal speech).

Diagnosis: Speech disorders are diagnosed by a speech-language pathologist (SLP) through evaluation techniques and speech samples.

Role of a Speech Coach: Focuses on improving communication skills, including speech clarity, fluency, and confidence in public speaking, without diagnosing medical conditions.

Coaching Techniques: Includes exercises for articulation, fluency strategies like slow speech and breathing, and voice training to improve pitch, volume, and resonance.

Career Opportunities: Speech coaches are in demand in schools, universities, private clinics, and corporate settings, especially for international students and individuals seeking speech improvement.

The field of sleep coaching in psychology can be highly beneficial. There is a growing demand for sleep coaches, yet the number of professionals in this area is still limited. After completing this course, you'll have the opportunity to take an additional course focused on becoming a certified sleep coach.

title: Speech Disorders
about: Speech disorders are conditions that hinder a person’s ability to produce sounds essential for effective communication. These disorders may arise due to issues with the muscles, nerves, or vocal structures, and include conditions like stuttering, apraxia, and dysarthria. Speech i
content:
Speech disorders are conditions that hinder a person’s ability to produce sounds essential for effective communication. These disorders may arise due to issues with the muscles, nerves, or vocal structures, and include conditions like stuttering, apraxia, and dysarthria. Speech is a primary mode of communication, relying on the coordinated effort of the head, neck, chest, and abdomen muscles.Speech disorders differ from language disorders in that they affect the production of sounds required for communication, while language disorders involve difficulties with understanding or using words. Both conditions can significantly impact an individual’s ability to express thoughts and emotions.

How do people speak
Speaking is a fascinating process that involves the cooperation of several parts of our body working together, all controlled by our brain. It all starts when we take a breath. We need to exhale air in order to produce sound, which is why we can't speak without blowing air out of our lungs. As we exhale, the air travels up through the trachea and into the larynx, also known as the voice box. Inside the larynx are the vocal cords—two small muscles that vibrate when the air passes through them. The vibrations create sound. The pitch of the sound is determined by how tight or loose the vocal cords are. When the cords are tightened, we produce a higher pitch, and when they are relaxed, the sound is deeper.

Once the sound is created in the vocal cords, it doesn’t just stop there. It travels upwards into the throat, mouth, and even the nasal passages. These spaces act as resonance chambers, shaping and amplifying the sound that was initially produced. The shape and size of your mouth, throat, and nose all affect how the sound is heard, creating the unique tones and sounds that form the vowels and consonants we use in speech.

At the same time, the movements in your mouth and tongue help articulate the sounds into distinct words. The lips, teeth, and tongue work together to form various sounds. For example, when you say "p," your lips come together; when you say "s," the air flows over your teeth. Your tongue plays a critical role in sounds like “t,” “d,” and “l.” These small movements, combined with the air and vibrations, are what allow us to form words and sentences that others can understand.

But all of this doesn’t happen automatically—it’s driven by the brain. The brain is responsible for selecting the words we want to say and putting them in the right order. It also sends signals to the muscles in the vocal cords, mouth, and tongue, directing them on how to move. The areas of the brain involved in this process include Broca’s area and Wernicke’s area, which handle language and speech production. In the end, speaking is an intricate dance between our brain, breath, vocal cords, and mouth muscles. We take a breath, exhale, and the air travels through our body, being shaped into meaningful words. It’s a skill that requires careful coordination, and without that exhaled air, speech would simply not be possible.

Speech Therapy 

Stuttering
Stuttering is one of the most recognized speech disorders, characterized by disruptions in the flow of speech. This includes issues with airflow, tightening of the vocal muscles, and irregular speech patterns.

Common Symptoms of Stuttering:

Repetitions: Unintentionally repeating sounds, syllables, words, or phrases.

Blocks: Struggling to produce speech sounds even though the person knows what they want to say.

Prolongations: Stretching certain sounds or syllables.

Physical and Behavioral Symptoms:

Tension in the face, neck, or shoulders.

Rapid blinking or lip tremors.

Clenched fists and involuntary head movements.

Types of Stuttering:

Developmental Stuttering: Common in children who are learning to speak; often hereditary.

Neurogenic Stuttering: Occurs due to brain damage that affects speech coordination, such as after a stroke or brain injury.

Stuttering can also lead to social anxiety and may impact a person’s confidence, making it more challenging to engage in conversations or public speaking.

Stuttering is common among young children as a normal part of learning to speak. Most Children outgrow this development stuttering.

Apraxia
Apraxia is a motor speech disorder in which the brain has difficulty sending the right signals to the muscles that control speech. This makes it hard for individuals to pronounce words correctly, even though they know what they want to say.

Dysarthria
Dysarthria is a motor speech disorder caused by weakness, paralysis, or lack of coordination of the muscles used for speech. It results from damage to the nervous system, typically the brain, and can affect the muscles involved in breathing, speaking, and controlling the vocal cords, lips, and tongue. People with dysarthria may have difficulty articulating words clearly, producing a voice that is too soft, slurred, or monotone.

Slow or rapid speech delivery.

Weak, hoarse, or breathy voice.

Difficulty moving the mouth, lips, or tongue.

General Symptoms of Speech Disorders

While symptoms can vary depending on the type of disorder, common issues include:

Repeating or prolonging sounds.

Distorted or rearranged syllables.

Speaking softly or with an unusual voice.

Difficulty pronouncing words correctly.

Slurred speech or difficulty pronouncing words

Causes of Speech Disorders

Therapist and child.

Speech disorders can stem from a variety of causes, including:

Brain damage (e.g., stroke, traumatic brain injury).

Muscle weakness or damage to the vocal cords.

Degenerative diseases (e.g., Parkinson’s disease, ALS).

Hearing impairments or memory loss.

Genetic conditions like autism or Down syndrome.

Premature birth or low birth weight.

Personal Story
My best friend in the Netherlands has always stuttered. We met in primary school and have been inseparable ever since. We went to secondary school together and even went on multiple holidays together. Stuttering has always been a part of his life. It’s not just a speech issue for him; it’s a condition that has shaped much of his experiences and interactions. One of the most difficult things to watch is when he struggles to get a word out. His stutter can sometimes last for up to 10 seconds, often over a single letter. The letter “T” is the worst for him. When it happens, you can see how much he suffers. His face turns red, he starts sweating, and it’s clear he’s fighting a battle with himself. He doesn't want to draw attention to it, but it’s impossible not to notice.

Speaking in front of a big group is especially tough. When he has to speak in front of people, whether it's in class, at work, or at a social event, the anxiety that builds up is overwhelming. Even answering a phone call can be an ordeal. It’s not just about saying words, it’s about the fear of judgment, the fear of not being understood, and the constant effort to communicate with ease.

But there’s one temporary relief for him, alcohol. When he has a drink, even just a little, it seems to loosen him up, and the stutter vanishes. When he’s tipsy, he becomes more talkative, and he can have whole conversations without the constant struggle. It’s a strange kind of “cure,” but it’s the only thing that seems to help him feel comfortable speaking. I remember a particular evening that highlighted just how deeply stuttering affects his life. His girlfriend, who’s a teacher, had a work event. She invited him, along with all the other partners. For him, it was going to be a nightmare. It wasn’t just a small get-together; it was a big gathering with her coworkers, all teachers. People were going to ask questions, expect him to talk, and he just didn’t know how he was going to handle it.

Hours before the party, he started drinking wine, just to calm his nerves and make sure he wouldn’t stutter when he got there. By the time he arrived, he’d already had two full bottles. He wasn’t drunk, but he was tipsy, and at that point, he felt confident. He had a beer with his girlfriend and her colleagues, thinking it would help him stay relaxed and able to join in the conversation. But things went terribly wrong. After a while, in front of the entire group of teachers, he suddenly threw up. It wasn’t because he had food poisoning or was sick, it was because the alcohol had gotten to him and it had hit him harder than expected.

The group rushed to help him, thinking he was just unwell, but they didn’t know the real reason behind it. They had no idea it was the alcohol causing the issue, not something he ate or some illness. And the thing is, he didn’t even want to be there in the first place. He had tried to numb the anxiety, and yet, it ended up making things worse. This experience really showed me that stuttering isn’t just about struggling to speak. It’s a condition that impacts so much more than just the words we say. It affects confidence, relationships, and social interactions in ways that others might not understand. My friend’s life is shaped by this constant challenge, and while alcohol may temporarily ease his struggle, it’s not a solution, it’s a way of coping with a condition that, for him, is a constant battle.

content:
Stuttering is a speech disorder that affects many individuals, making it difficult for them to produce speech smoothly and fluently. While various treatments, including speech therapy and support groups like the National Stuttering Association® (NSA), have shown benefits, there is currently no cure for stuttering. Researchers are exploring new treatments, such as electronic devices, pharmaceuticals, and other alternative therapies, but no definitive cure has been found yet.

It’s important to understand that it is unrealistic to expect any treatment to make stuttering completely disappear. What works for one person may not work for another, and relapses are common. For effective management, it’s essential to approach stuttering with patience and understanding. The most successful support often starts with acceptance of the stuttering itself, which can be challenging but is crucial to overcoming its emotional impact.

Reducing Disfluency
Fluency shaping is a treatment method aimed at reducing disfluency, which involves working with a speech-language pathologist (SLP) to modify speech patterns. The goal is to eliminate stuttering events and achieve consistent fluent speech. Some therapies also incorporate assistive devices, such as delayed auditory feedback, to support the process.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is another method frequently used to treat stuttering. This multidisciplinary approach addresses the emotional, behavioral, and cognitive aspects of stuttering. While CBT can be helpful for managing the anxiety and frustration associated with stuttering, it’s important to note that it does not offer a cure.

While fluency shaping and delayed auditory feedback may work well for some individuals, these methods may not always be effective or sustainable. They focus on eliminating stuttering but might overlook the emotional and psychological factors that also contribute to communication challenges.

The Importance of Early Intervention
Though no universally accepted treatment exists, early intervention is widely agreed upon by clinicians as a key to better outcomes. If stuttering is identified in a young child, they should be referred to an SLP for a thorough evaluation. Research indicates that early treatment significantly reduces the likelihood that stuttering will persist into adulthood.

By addressing disfluencies early, children can avoid developing negative emotional reactions, tension, and speech avoidance behaviors that often worsen stuttering. Many early intervention programs also offer support to parents and caregivers, helping them navigate the process with their child.

No Cure, But Progress is Possible

It’s important to remember that no single technique, device, or medication will cure stuttering. Often, people who stutter are told to “slow down” or “just relax,” but these well-intentioned suggestions oversimplify the issue. Stuttering is not a matter of anxiety or lack of control. It’s a neurological condition that requires individualized treatment. Working with an SLP is essential to address each person’s unique communication needs.

Speech therapy is like discovery

Minimizing the Impact of Stuttering
In addition to fluency shaping, stuttering modification is another treatment approach focused on reducing the impact of stuttering. This technique involves identifying and adjusting disfluencies as they occur. With the help of an SLP, people who stutter can learn to reduce physical tension, overcome the fear of speaking, and use strategies to manage their speech in real time.

Stuttering modification also incorporates counseling to reduce anxiety and help individuals feel more comfortable speaking. Techniques for shortening and easing stuttering moments are integral to this approach, allowing people to communicate more effectively.

What Makes Treatment Successful?
The success of treatment is dependent on the individual's personal goals, feelings, and attitudes toward their stuttering. Today, most treatment programs combine various methods to create a tailored approach. Successful treatment should help individuals manage their emotions, reduce stress around speaking, and participate more comfortably in daily activities. To this end, SLPs may also promote self-advocacy, offer counseling strategies, and involve families in the treatment process.

The Role of Support Groups
Support groups for people who stutter provide a valuable space for information, encouragement, and a sense of community. Attending a support group can help individuals gain new perspectives on fluency, speak without fear of judgment, and learn how to explain their condition to others. Many participants report feeling more confident in their speaking abilities and more at ease knowing they’re not alone. For some, joining groups like those run by the NSA can be a life-changing experience, boosting their confidence and comfort level.

Tips for Parents and Teachers
Parents and teachers can play a key role in supporting students who stutter. Here are some helpful guidelines:

1
Don’t tell the student to “slow down” or “just relax.” These comments may unintentionally increase their anxiety.

2
Don’t finish their sentences or speak for them. Give them the space to express themselves.

3
Encourage turn-taking in conversations and ensure all students have equal speaking opportunities.

4
Speak with the student in a relaxed, unhurried manner. Pausing frequently allows the student time to process and respond.

5
Focus on the message, not how it is spoken. Encourage clear communication over fluency.

6
Have private conversations with the student about accommodations they may need without emphasizing their stuttering.

7
Normalize stuttering by discussing it openly. Treat it as a natural aspect of communication and ensure it is not a source of shame.

Moving Forward

Stuttering is a lifelong challenge for many, but with the right treatment and support, individuals can live full, effective lives. No single solution works for everyone, but progress is possible with a combination of speech therapy, emotional support, and practical strategies for managing speech. By understanding and accepting stuttering, we can help create a more inclusive and supportive environment for those who face this condition.

title: Facts and Myths
about:
Myth: Speech disorders are only about stuttering.

Fact: Speech disorders include a wide range of conditions, such as stuttering, articulation disorders, voice disorders, and aphasia, which affect different aspects of speech, including fluency, clarity, and vocal quality.

Myth:
content:
Myth: Speech disorders are only about stuttering.

Fact: Speech disorders include a wide range of conditions, such as stuttering, articulation disorders, voice disorders, and aphasia, which affect different aspects of speech, including fluency, clarity, and vocal quality.

Myth: Children will outgrow speech disorders on their own.

Fact: While some children may naturally overcome speech issues as they develop, many speech disorders require early intervention and ongoing therapy for the best outcomes.

Myth: Speech disorders are always caused by developmental issues.

Fact: Speech disorders can result from various causes, including neurological conditions, brain injuries, hearing loss, cleft palate, or emotional trauma, in addition to developmental delays.

Myth: People with speech disorders are less intelligent.

Fact: Speech disorders do not reflect intelligence. Many individuals with speech disorders are highly intelligent and capable but may face challenges in expressing themselves clearly due to their condition.

Myth: Therapy for speech disorders is only about fixing the speech.

Fact: Speech therapy addresses more than just speech production. It also helps individuals with communication strategies, social skills, confidence, and emotional support related to their speech difficulties.

Myth: Stuttering is caused by nervousness or anxiety.

Fact: While anxiety can exacerbate stuttering, it is not the cause. Stuttering is a complex speech disorder that involves disruptions in the flow of speech due to neurological and genetic factors.

Myth: Speech disorders only affect children.

Fact: Speech disorders can affect individuals of all ages, from children to adults. In fact, some speech disorders may not be diagnosed until later in life.

Myth: People with speech disorders can’t get better.

Fact: Many people with speech disorders can make significant improvements with appropriate therapy and support. Early intervention often leads to better outcomes.

Myth: People with speech disorders have trouble with reading and writing.

Fact: A speech disorder does not necessarily affect a person’s reading and writing abilities. However, in some cases, there may be overlap with language or learning disorders.

Myth: Speech disorders are always visible.

Fact: Some speech disorders, like aphasia or voice disorders, may not have visible signs but can still significantly affect a person’s ability to communicate effectively.

Career options related to addiction in Vietnam are promising, as addiction is a growing concern in the country. Common addictions include alcohol, gambling, and screen addiction (especially social media). Screen addiction, in particular, is a significant issue globally, with the younger generation spending increasing amounts of time on social media platforms. This can have a profound impact on mental health, social relationships, and productivity. In Vietnam, the demand for addiction coaches and specialists is on the rise, especially as more individuals and families seek help to manage and overcome these addictive behaviors. As a coach, you can offer support to individuals struggling with addiction by helping them set goals, develop healthier habits, and navigate the challenges they face. You can also provide guidance and counseling to families, helping them understand the impact of addiction and how they can better support their loved ones. Overall, the field of addiction coaching presents significant opportunities in Vietnam, particularly for professionals who are equipped with knowledge and expertise in dealing with addiction and its psychological effects. By providing coaching and support, you can help individuals and families build healthier, more balanced lives.

Key Points
Types of Addiction: Understanding common addictions like alcohol, gambling, and screen/social media addiction.

Causes of Addiction: Exploring psychological, social, and environmental factors that contribute to addictive behaviors.

Signs and Symptoms: Identifying key indicators of addiction, such as withdrawal, loss of control, and negative impact on daily life.

Effects of Addiction: Examining the physical, mental, and social consequences of addiction on individuals and their families.

Treatment and Support: Overview of strategies for managing and overcoming addiction, including therapy, support groups, and lifestyle changes.

title: What is Addiction?
about: Many people view addiction as a result of personal weakness, initially for self-gratification, which continues due to a lack of willpower to stop. However, in the medical and scientific community, the perspective that pleasure-seeking leads to addiction is no longer widely accept
content:
Many people view addiction as a result of personal weakness, initially for self-gratification, which continues due to a lack of willpower to stop. However, in the medical and scientific community, the perspective that pleasure-seeking leads to addiction is no longer widely accepted. Today, clinicians and scientists believe that many people engage in potentially addictive activities to escape discomfort, both physical and mental. People often seek neuro-stimulating experiences to feel better and improve their mood. The origins of addiction lie in activities related to sensation-seeking and self-soothing.

In everyday conversations, people often mention addiction casually. They might call themselves a "chocolate addict" or a "workaholic." However, addiction is not a term clinicians take lightly. You might be surprised to learn that the term addiction didn’t appear in any edition of the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) until the fifth edition (DSM-5), which is the reference book clinicians use to diagnose and classify mental health disorders. In this recent edition, addiction is included as a category and encompasses both substance use disorders and non-substance addictions, such as alcohol use disorder and gambling disorder. In short, addiction is defined as the inability to stop doing, taking, or using something to the extent that it may harm you. Addiction is often associated with gambling, sex, drugs, alcohol, and smoking, but it can apply to almost anything, including:

Work: Some people are so obsessed with their work that they experience physical exhaustion; if your relationships, family, and social life are affected and you never take time off, you may have a work addiction.

Internet: With the rise in computer and mobile phone use, internet addiction has increased as well; people can spend hours a day online or gaming, neglecting other aspects of life.

Solvents: Volatile substance abuse involves inhaling items like glue, aerosol cans, gasoline, or lighter fuel to induce a sense of euphoria.

Shopping: Shopping becomes an addiction when you buy things you don’t need or want simply to feel excitement; this often leads to feelings of guilt, shame, or despair.

How Does Addiction Work?
It may seem odd to classify gambling problems in the same category as drug or alcohol issues. But addiction specialists are moving away from the idea that each addiction corresponds to a specific substance or activity. Instead, the Addiction Syndrome Model suggests that there is a single addiction with multiple manifestations. The addictive object could be almost anything—either a substance or a non-drug activity. For addiction to develop, the substance or activity must shift one’s subjective experience in a desired direction—feeling good or feeling better.

Advances in science have shaped our understanding of this complex and common issue. For instance, brain imaging technology has shown that our brains respond similarly to different pleasurable experiences, whether from substances like alcohol and drugs or behaviors like gambling, shopping, and sex. Genetic research has revealed that some people have a predisposition to addiction but are not necessarily inclined toward a specific type of addiction.

These findings suggest that the addictive object (whether a substance or behavior) is less significant than previously thought. Instead, new thinking reflects the belief that addiction is functional: it serves a purpose but has destructive effects. Addiction is the relationship between a person and an object or activity. In addiction, the object or activity becomes increasingly important, while previously important activities become less so. Ultimately, addiction is a complex struggle between acting on an urge and resisting it. When this struggle causes distress in health, family, work, or other daily activities, it can lead to addiction.

Cycle of addition.

What Causes Addictions?
There are many reasons why addiction begins. In the case of drugs, alcohol, and nicotine, these substances alter how you feel both physically and mentally. These sensations can be enjoyable and create a strong urge to reuse the substance. Gambling can lead to a similar "high" after a win, followed by a powerful urge to recreate that feeling. This can develop into a difficult-to-break habit. Being addicted to something means experiencing withdrawal symptoms or "crashing" without it. Because this can be uncomfortable, it’s easier to keep using or doing what you crave, continuing the cycle. Typically, addiction can spiral out of control because you increasingly need more of it to satisfy your craving and achieve a "high."

How Addiction Can Impact Life
The stress of managing addiction can severely harm an individual's work life and relationships. In cases of substance abuse (e.g., drugs and alcohol), addiction can cause serious psychological and physical impacts. Some studies show that a person’s risk of addiction is partly genetic, but environmental factors, such as being around others who are addicted, are also thought to increase the risk of addiction. Behaviors like substance abuse may serve as a coping mechanism for difficult issues. Unemployment and poverty can lead to addiction, along with stress and emotional or occupational pressure.

Addition is often a life struggle

There Are Many Paths to Recovery from Addiction, and Each Takes Time
Addiction is a chronic, often relapsing disorder. It often precedes other emotional issues. However, people can and do recover from addiction on their own. If not on their own, they may recover with the help of social networks or treatment providers. Recovery from addiction often requires significant effort. This can lead to feelings of frustration and helplessness. Smoking is often seen as one of the hardest addictions to overcome. However, the vast majority of smokers have quit on their own! Others have quit smoking with the help of professional treatment. Remember, overcoming addiction often requires many efforts. Each attempt provides an important learning opportunity that shapes the experience and, despite challenges, brings those in recovery closer to their goals. There are many paths to addiction and many to recovery. Think of recovery from addiction as a five-year journey with ups and downs; after about five years, life can and will be very different. As life becomes more fulfilling, addiction loses its grip.

title: Alcohol and Drug Addiction
about: Abuse of substances such as alcohol, marijuana, cocaine, prescription drugs, and others can lead to serious health issues and cause significant problems with family, friends, coworkers, work, finances, and the law. Despite these consequences, substance use often continues. ​Alcoh
content:
Abuse of substances such as alcohol, marijuana, cocaine, prescription drugs, and others can lead to serious health issues and cause significant problems with family, friends, coworkers, work, finances, and the law. Despite these consequences, substance use often continues. ​Alcohol consumption in Vietnam has reached concerning levels, significantly impacting public health and social well-being.

Why Does This Happen?
Addiction is a physical dependency on a chemical substance, which leads to uncomfortable withdrawal symptoms when the substance is stopped. People may initially begin using substances because they provide a pleasurable experience. However, as addiction develops, the pleasure fades, and the drive to continue using substances shifts toward avoiding unpleasant withdrawal symptoms. These substances can cause both physical and psychological harm, often leading to antisocial behavior. Antisocial behavior may escalate into criminal activity, either when a person is under the influence of a substance or when they need money to buy the substance to which they are addicted. Depression is also common among substance users.

The Genetic Factor
Addiction has a strong genetic component. For example, children who are raised apart from their biological alcoholic parents are four times more likely to become alcoholics than the general population. This suggests that different individuals have varying levels of susceptibility to addiction. While one person may drink socially without becoming addicted, another may develop a dependency. It remains a mystery why this happens. People who are prone to addiction to one substance often develop dependencies on other substances as well. Environmental factors, such as physical or sexual abuse, or adverse social conditions, also contribute to addiction. However, addiction can affect individuals from all social classes. While addiction leads to personality changes over time, there is no specific personality trait that can predict the development of addictive behaviors.

Alcohol Use
Alcohol abuse can fall into one of three categories:

Daily consumption with intoxication.

Drinking at specific, predictable times.

Extended periods of abstinence followed by binge drinking, which may last days, weeks, or even months.

Chronic alcoholism is a progressive disease that typically develops in stages, often beginning between the ages of 20 and 40. First Stage: Drinking to relieve stress and the beginning of physical dependency on alcohol. Second Stage: Increasing preoccupation with drinking, loss of control, and potential blackouts. Third Stage: Behavioral and personality changes, including aggression and extreme denial of the problem. In the late stages, continued alcohol use severely impairs physical and mental health, impacting a person’s ability to function.

Physical Complications 
Long-term alcohol abuse increases the risk of pneumonia, tuberculosis, heart failure, and liver failure (cirrhosis). Alcohol poisoning is a major cause of motor vehicle accidents and other injuries. Pregnant women who drink may cause fetal alcohol syndrome, leading to intellectual disabilities in the child. Alcohol withdrawal symptoms can include restlessness, agitation, hallucinations, delirium, and seizures. In severe cases, withdrawal can be life-threatening and may require hospitalization.

The dark side of alcohol

Alcohol addiction treatment
Effective treatment for alcohol addiction involves a combination of medical, therapeutic, and support-based approaches. Here are the main treatment options:

1. Detoxification

The first step in treating alcohol addiction is often detoxification, which helps individuals safely withdraw from alcohol under medical supervision. Withdrawal symptoms can be severe, so detox may require hospitalization.

2. Medications

Several medications can assist in reducing cravings and preventing relapse:

Disulfiram (Antabuse): Causes unpleasant effects (e.g., nausea) when alcohol is consumed, discouraging drinking.

Acamprosate (Campral): Reduces alcohol cravings and helps maintain sobriety.

Naltrexone (Revia, Vivitrol): Blocks the pleasurable effects of alcohol and reduces cravings.

3. Behavioral Therapy

Therapy is crucial for addressing the psychological aspects of addiction. Key therapies include:

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): Helps individuals identify and change negative thought patterns related to alcohol use.

Motivational Interviewing (MI): Encourages individuals to explore their motivations for change and increase their commitment to sobriety.

Contingency Management: Provides rewards for staying sober.

4. Support Groups

12-Step Programs (e.g., Alcoholics Anonymous): These programs offer peer support, encouragement, and a structured path to recovery through regular meetings and a 12-step process.

Sober Living Programs: These residential programs provide supportive environments to help individuals transition back into daily life while maintaining sobriety.

5. Inpatient and Outpatient Rehabilitation

Inpatient Rehab: Intensive, residential treatment where individuals receive 24/7 care and support. It is ideal for those with severe addiction.

Outpatient Rehab: Flexible treatment for those who do not require full-time care, involving regular therapy sessions and support meetings.

Mental Effects of Alcohol on the Brain

Tobacco Use
Nicotine addiction can develop quickly through smoking cigarettes, cigars, pipes, chewing tobacco, or using snuff. Nicotine is one of the most addictive substances, and addiction develops rapidly. It is often harder to quit smoking than to quit other drugs like cocaine or heroin. Tobacco is easily accessible, relatively inexpensive, and socially accepted (though this is changing). Nicotine doesn’t make you "high," and it doesn’t impair your ability to function, making it easier to ignore its harmful effects. Smoking reinforces the addiction through regular, repetitive behavior.

Tobacco use is a leading cause of death in the United States, accounting for about 1 in 7 deaths overall, and 1 in 3 deaths between the ages of 35 and 70. Smoking is a major risk factor for chronic bronchitis, emphysema, heart disease, and various cancers, including lung, mouth, and throat cancer. Smoking also raises blood pressure, increases blood clotting, and damages arteries, contributing to more deaths from heart disease than from cancer.

Treatment Options
1. Nicotine Replacement Therapy (NRT)

NRT helps manage withdrawal by providing a controlled dose of nicotine. Available forms include: Patches, Gum, Lozenges, Nasal spray, Inhalers. NRT reduces cravings and withdrawal symptoms.

2. Prescription Medications

Bupropion: Reduces cravings and withdrawal symptoms.

Varenicline: Blocks nicotine receptors and reduces cravings.

Both medications help people quit smoking and manage withdrawal.

3. Behavioral Therapy

Therapy focuses on identifying triggers and breaking smoking habits. This includes:

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)

Counseling

Motivational Interviewing

Support groups and smoking cessation programs also provide valuable support.

4. Support Programs

Quitlines offer phone-based counseling.

Nicotine Anonymous is a 12-step program.

Apps and online resources offer interactive tools for support.

5. Alternative Therapies

Hypnotherapy and acupuncture may help, though their effectiveness is less proven.

Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome
Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome (WKS) is a brain disorder caused by a severe deficiency in thiamine (vitamin B1), which is essential for converting food into energy. A lack of thiamine can lead to significant brain damage. WKS occurs in two stages:

Wernicke Encephalopathy: An acute brain disorder.

Korsakoff Syndrome: A long-term memory disorder.

The condition is named after Carl Wernicke and Sergei Korsakoff, neurologists who studied it.

How Are Wernicke Encephalopathy and Korsakoff Syndrome Related?

If left untreated, Wernicke encephalopathy can progress to Korsakoff syndrome. Early symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy include confusion, impaired motor coordination, and vision problems. If untreated, it can cause lasting brain and nerve damage, leading to the memory loss seen in Korsakoff syndrome. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is more common in men, particularly those aged 30 to 70 years, and is frequently linked to alcohol use disorder. However, it can also develop in women and younger individuals due to other causes, though it is rare in children.

Key Risk Factors for WKS include:

1
Alcohol use disorder (which impairs thiamine absorption)

2
Malnutrition or conditions that limit nutrient absorption (e.g., gastrointestinal diseases)

3
Chronic conditions like cancer, HIV/AIDS, thyroid problems, and kidney failure

4
Limited access to medical care or healthy food

Alcohol addiction is very strong addiction.

How Common is Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome?
Approximately 2% of people worldwide develop WKS. Around 50% of those with Wernicke encephalopathy progress to Korsakoff syndrome, with a higher rate (80%) among those with alcohol use disorder. The primary cause is thiamine deficiency, often due to chronic alcohol use, which impairs thiamine absorption. Other causes include poor nutrition, eating disorders, chronic infections, surgery, and head injuries.

title: Gambling Addiction
about: Gambling in moderation is generally seen as socially acceptable. However, gambling addiction is a serious problem that can severely impact your finances, relationships, and overall well-being. If left untreated, it can cause significant harm in various aspects of your life. The N
content:
Gambling in moderation is generally seen as socially acceptable. However, gambling addiction is a serious problem that can severely impact your finances, relationships, and overall well-being. If left untreated, it can cause significant harm in various aspects of your life. The National Council on Problem Gambling reports that over 2% of Americans suffer from problem gambling. Those struggling with addiction may feel an uncontrollable urge to buy lottery tickets, visit casinos, bet on sports, or gamble online. While the type and frequency of gambling may differ, the common thread is a lack of control. Even when facing negative consequences like social, financial, or legal issues, the urge to gamble persists. Although gambling addiction is more common among men, women are increasingly affected.

Gambling in Vietnam
While gambling has been illegal in Vietnam for centuries, the country is now facing growing issues with gambling addiction. Most gambling activities, particularly sports betting, occur online. People often place bets on things like goals, winners, and penalties. A study indicates that over 53% of the Vietnamese population engages in activities like sports betting or buying lottery tickets at times. Globally, up to 5% of adolescents and young adults who gamble develop a gambling disorder. Men are twice as likely as women to be affected, though the number of women with gambling problems is rising.

Signs of Gambling Addiction
Gambling addiction can be hard to hide. Even if you try to keep it private, signs often show in other areas of life. Some common indicators include obsessing over gambling, using gambling as an escape or to feel better, inability to control gambling behavior, neglecting work or responsibilities to gamble, using money meant for bills or essential expenses to gamble, selling belongings or stealing money to fund gambling, lying about gambling habits, feeling guilty after gambling, and taking larger risks while gambling. Gambling addiction can lead to destroyed relationships and friendships, loss of possessions such as your house, job, or car, and emotional distress, guilt, and shame. Even if gambling doesn’t happen frequently, when it does, individuals may struggle to stop once they begin.

Symptoms of Gambling Addiction
Gambling addiction can be difficult to conceal. People with this addiction may try to hide their behavior, but signs often emerge in other aspects of life. You may need frequent access to casinos or online gambling platforms. Even if you gamble privately at home, your addiction may manifest in various ways. Some signs of gambling addiction include:

1
Obsessing over gambling

2
Gambling to escape or feel better about life

3
Inability to control gambling habits

4
Neglecting work or other commitments to gamble

5
Using money meant for bills or expenses to gamble

6
Selling possessions or stealing money to fund gambling

7
Lying about gambling habits

8
Feeling guilty after gambling sessions

9
Taking increasingly larger risks while gambling

Most of the people get bankrupt.

Treatment for Gambling Addiction
With proper treatment, gambling addiction is manageable. Unlike other addictions, gambling is not necessary for survival, but learning to develop a healthy relationship with money is essential. Completely quitting gambling is important, as even occasional gambling can trigger a relapse. Treatment methods for gambling addiction are similar to those for other types of addiction: Inpatient Rehabilitation: Some individuals benefit from structured inpatient programs, which may last from 30 days to a year, depending on addiction severity. Outpatient Rehabilitation: A more common option where individuals attend therapy and support groups while living at home and continuing daily life activities. Twelve-Step Programs: Programs like Gamblers Anonymous (GA) offer peer support and group meetings to help individuals recover from gambling addiction. Psychotherapy/Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): Therapy is crucial to address emotional or psychological issues that may contribute to gambling addiction. CBT helps individuals change self-destructive behaviors and develop healthier coping strategies. Medication: In some cases, medication may be needed to address underlying mental health conditions like bipolar disorder that fuel gambling urges.

A lot of gambling through card games.

A Personal story
It was November 22, 2023, around 1:45 p.m. when Cuong and Tri, both wearing face masks and helmets, arrived at a bank on a motorbike, according to the indictment. Then, on December 28, 2023, I read the heartbreaking news: Cuong, from Quang Nam Province, received the death penalty, while Tri, a native of Da Nang, was sentenced to 30 years in prison. The charges? The two young men robbed a bank in Da Nang, and during the robbery, Cuong fatally stabbed the bank's security guard. This happened very close to my home. I feel deeply for the victim’s family. My emotions are mixed: sadness, anger, and, oddly enough, a sense of relief that the punishment is severe.

You might think, "The court has decided, let’s move on with our lives." But as someone working in mental health, this situation is both tragic and all too familiar. The story behind these actions isn't unique, it’s something I’ve seen before. From what I've gathered, the two young men were approached by someone offering them a large sum of money, with the promise that if they used it wisely and were lucky in gambling, they could live the life they had always dreamed of, wealth, status, and the glamorous lifestyle they see on social media. These boys, young and naive, took the money and began gambling. Unfortunately, luck was not on their side. Instead, they became trapped in a situation where winning was practically impossible. In just one day, they found themselves buried in a debt of 200 million dong (the exact amount is unclear). Panic set in. The lender threatened them, saying if they didn’t pay back the debt, they would harm their family members, even threatening to rape their sister. The boys, already in panic, felt helpless and overwhelmed by stress.

Now, let’s zoom out and reflect on this situation. Ask yourself these questions: 

Do you think these boys woke up that day intending to kill someone?

Do you think they wanted to harm the security guard?

If they had not been in such a state of panic, do you think they would have even considered robbing the bank?

I believe the answer to all of these questions is No. As a professional, I feel a profound sense of sadness about the situation and even about the punishment they received. These two young men had so much potential. They could still study, play soccer, and work. Yet, one received the death penalty, and the other 30 years in prison, not for premeditated murder, but because of a risky decision they made weeks earlier related to gambling.

Whatever your opinion is on this matter, I challenge you to step out of your emotional reaction and look at it from a professional perspective. Two young, naive men were approached by a figure who offered them a dangerous opportunity. They gambled, and the pressure to repay a crushing debt was unbearable. In a desperate moment, they decided to rob a bank. They had no experience with crime, no criminal background, and no control over the situation. The result? Panic and stress and a security guard’s death.

As a professional, you can judge the outcome, but it’s more important to understand where this outcome came from. With the right support, this could have been avoided. Two lives lost, one destroyed by 30 years in prison, families in pain, these are the consequences of a lack of guidance and intervention at a critical time or even good education about gambling and risks. With a little support and proper mental health care, this tragedy could have been prevented.

Unfortunately, this situation is not unique. I know of numerous instances around me where people find themselves in the same cycle. Gambling, borrowing money, and then, regret, shame, stress, panic, and sometimes even being abandoned by their families. In my opinion, the real criminals aren’t the ones who take the money and take the risk. The real criminals are those who provide the money, trapping people in a horrific situation from which it’s nearly impossible to escape.
