title: Conduct Disorder
about: Conduct disorder (CD) is a mental health condition that affects children and teens that’s characterized by a consistent pattern of aggressive behaviors and actions that harm the well-being of others. Children with conduct disorder also often violate rules and societal norms. Cond
content:
Conduct disorder (CD) is a mental health condition that affects children and teens that’s characterized by a consistent pattern of aggressive behaviors and actions that harm the well-being of others. Children with conduct disorder also often violate rules and societal norms. Conduct disorder lies on a spectrum of disruptive behavioral disorders, which also includes oppositional defiant disorder (ODD). In some cases, ODD leads to CD. Conduct disorder often occurs alongside other psychiatric conditions, including:

Depression.

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

Learning disorders.

What is the difference between conduct disorder and personality disorders?
A personality disorder is a mental health condition that involves long-lasting, disruptive patterns of thinking, behavior, mood and relating to others. Most personality disorders begin in the teen years around 10-18 years, when personality further develops and matures. As a result, almost all people diagnosed with personality disorders are above the age of 18. There’s not much difference between conduct disorder (CD) and a personality disorder (PD), but CD is typically diagnosed in children. If an adult meets the criteria for both conditions, then a mental health professional would give them a diagnosis of PD instead of CD.

How common is conduct disorder?
Conduct disorder affects anywhere between 2% and 10% of children and adolescents worldwide. Characteristic behaviors of conduct disorder develop gradually over time. Children with conduct disorder tend to be impulsive and difficult to manage. They don’t seem to be concerned about the feelings of other people.

Conduct disorder in children

The four core behaviors of conduct disorder include:
1. Aggression toward people and animals and/or violating others’ basic rights.

2. Destruction of property.

3. Deceiving, lying and/or stealing.

4. Serious violations of rules.

1. Signs of aggressive behavior toward others include:

Bullying.

Physical violence (potentially with a weapon).

Verbal fights.

Threatening.

Forcing sexual activity.

Blaming others for their own behavior.

Hurting animals.

Intentionally setting fires.

2. Destruction of property.

Vandalizing or destroying others’ property.

3. Signs of deceiving, lying and stealing include:

Lying to get a favor or to avoid responsibilities.

Stealing from individual people or stores.

Breaking into houses or businesses.

4. Signs of violations of rules include:

Breaking rules without clear reason.

Not going to school (truancy).

Running away from home.

Frequently breaking any rules set by their parents.

Other common signs of conduct disorder include:

1
Heavy alcohol drinking and/or heavy substance use.

2
Engaging in frequent and risky sex.

3
Becoming easily frustrated.

4
Making no effort to hide their aggressive behaviors.

5
Not showing remorse for their actions.

6
Difficulty making and maintaining friendships.

It’s important to note that occasional rebellious behavior is common during childhood and adolescence. The signs and symptoms that lead to the diagnosis of conduct disorder demonstrate a disruptive and repetitive pattern.

Signs of conduct disorder in adults
Adults who have conduct disorder may have difficulty keeping a job or maintaining relationships. They may be prone to illegal or dangerous behavior. Symptoms of conduct disorder in an adult may be diagnosed as antisocial personality disorder. Researchers aren’t sure what exactly causes conduct disorder (CD), but they think it’s a complex combination of genetic/biological and environmental factors.

An example of conduct disorder

Genetic/biological factors:

Various studies show that certain characteristics of CD can be inherited, including antisocial behavior, impulsivity, temperament, aggression and insensitivity to punishment.

High testosterone levels are associated with aggression.

Traumatic brain injury, seizures and neurological damage can contribute to aggression.

Parental, familial and environmental factors:

Parents of adolescents with CD often have engaged in substance use and antisocial behaviors. They’re also frequently diagnosed with ADHD, mood disorders, schizophrenia or antisocial personality disorder.

A home environment that lacks structure and adequate supervision with frequent conflicts between parents can lead to maladaptive behavior in children, which can lead to CD.

Children exposed to frequent domestic violence are more likely to develop CD.

Living in low social and economic environments with overcrowding and unemployment leads to economic and social stress with a lack of adequate parenting. CD affects more children living in low economic environments than not.

Availability of drugs and increased crime in a child’s neighborhood increases their risk of developing CD.

It’s important to note that conduct disorder can occur in children from high-functioning, healthy families.

How is conduct disorder treated?
The go-to treatment for conduct disorder (CD) is multiple forms of psychotherapy (talk therapy) for your child and family, as well as community-based treatment. Therapies include:

Parent management training
The goal of this therapy is to train the child’s parents to set consistent discipline with proper rewarding of positive behaviors.

Psychotherapy
“Psychotherapy” is a term for a variety of treatment techniques that aim to help a person identify and change troubling emotions, thoughts and behaviors. Working with a mental health professional can provide support, education and guidance to the person and their family. Psychotherapy for conduct disorder usually needs to target family life and school with a focus on improving family dynamics, academic functioning and improving your child’s behavior in the context of various environments.

Anger management training
The goal of anger management is to reduce both your child’s emotional feelings and the physiological arousal that anger causes. You can’t get rid of or totally avoid the things or people that make them angry, so anger management training teaches your child how to control their reactions.

Individual psychotherapy
Individual therapy for a child with conduct disorder focuses on developing problem-solving skills, strengthening relationships by resolving conflicts and learning skills to decline negative influences in their environment.

Community-based treatment
This treatment involves therapeutic schools and residential treatment centers that can provide a structured program to reduce disruptive behaviors.

Healthcare providers typically don’t use medication to directly treat conduct disorder, but as other mental health conditions often occur alongside conduct disorder, your child may benefit from medication to manage these conditions.

Prevention
At this time, there’s no known way to prevent conduct disorder, as it’s likely caused by a complex combination of factors, but many of the related problems might be lessened with treatment. Seeking help as soon as symptoms appear can help decrease the disruption to your child’s life, family and friendships.

Career opportunities in therapy may not always be immediately obvious. Key Points
Psychology: Learning about various therapies gives you a deeper understanding of psychological concepts, human behavior, and emotional well-being.

Useful for Coaching: Knowledge of therapeutic approaches can enhance your ability to guide and support individuals as a coach, especially when helping clients manage challenges or improve their mental health.

Different Therapeutic Approaches: You’ll be exposed to a wide range of therapies, including Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), Psychoanalysis, Gestalt Therapy, and more, each with its own methods and applications.

content:
1. Psychoanalysis & Psychodynamic Therapy

A session between a therapist and a client

Focus: The focus is on uncovering unconscious thoughts, past experiences, and unresolved conflicts, particularly those from childhood, that influence current behavior. It delves into the deep structure of the mind, including repressed memories and desires.How It’s Done: Sessions typically involve free association (where the patient speaks freely without censoring their thoughts), dream analysis, and exploring early life experiences. The therapist creates a safe space to encourage openness. The relationship between the patient and therapist is also examined, often revealing unresolved emotional issues (transference). Psychoanalysis can be long-term, lasting several years.

2. Interpersonal Therapy
Focus: The focus is on improving interpersonal relationships and social functioning. It emphasizes the connection between mood disorders (like depression) and problematic relationships or life events.How It’s Done: The therapist helps the patient identify and explore personal relationships, significant life events, and how these affect emotional health. By improving communication and addressing unresolved relational issues, the patient gains better emotional regulation. Sessions are typically short-term (around 12–16 weeks) and solution-focused.

3. Mentalization Therapy
Focus: The focus is on enhancing the ability to understand one’s own emotions and how they influence behavior, as well as recognizing others’ emotions and how they impact relationships.How It’s Done: The therapist works with the patient to explore the connection between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, especially in social contexts. It's often used for borderline personality disorder. The therapy involves questioning, reflection, and role-playing to improve mentalization and emotional regulation.

4. Family Therapy

Focus: The focus is on addressing and improving communication, behavior patterns, and dynamics within the family unit. It explores how individual behaviors affect the entire family.How It’s Done: Family members meet together in therapy sessions. The therapist helps identify dysfunctional patterns, facilitates communication, and teaches conflict resolution strategies. The therapy may include problem-solving exercises, role-playing, and discussions of family history. It’s often short-term and targeted towards resolving specific issues.

Family therapy, includes every family member.

5. Group Therapy
Focus: The focus is on creating a safe environment where individuals can share their experiences, gain support, and learn from others. It’s often used for social support, skill-building, and education on specific topics (like addiction or grief).How It’s Done: A group of patients, typically 6–15 people, meets with one or two therapists. Participants discuss their challenges, provide feedback, and support one another. The therapist may guide the group through structured exercises or facilitate discussion around specific themes. It’s especially useful for those who feel isolated or want to connect with others facing similar issues.

6. Behavioral Therapy
Focus: The focus is on changing observable behaviors through reinforcement or punishment techniques. It’s grounded in the idea that behavior is learned and can be unlearned.How It’s Done: Therapists work with patients to identify target behaviors and then create a plan to reinforce desirable behaviors while reducing unwanted ones. Techniques like positive reinforcement, modeling, and conditioning (e.g., classical or operant conditioning) are used. It’s often short-term and goal-oriented.

7. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)
Focus: The focus is on identifying and challenging unhelpful or irrational thoughts that influence emotions and behaviors. It seeks to change patterns of thinking to improve emotional well-being.How It’s Done: The therapist works with the patient to recognize distorted thoughts (like catastrophizing or all-or-nothing thinking) and replace them with balanced, realistic alternatives. Patients practice these new thinking patterns both in and outside therapy, often through homework assignments. CBT is often short-term and structured.

8. Exposure Therapy
Focus: The focus is on helping individuals gradually face their fears and anxieties in a controlled, safe environment. This helps reduce avoidance and promotes healthier responses to distressing stimuli.How It’s Done: The therapist guides the patient in exposing them to feared situations, starting with less threatening scenarios and gradually working up to more challenging ones. The goal is to reduce fear and anxiety through repeated exposure, while teaching coping strategies.

9. Mindfulness-Based Therapy
Focus: The focus is on cultivating present-moment awareness and acceptance of one’s thoughts, emotions, and bodily sensations. It helps patients manage stress, anxiety, and depression.How It’s Done: The therapist teaches mindfulness practices, such as meditation, breathing exercises, and body scanning. The goal is to help the patient become more aware of their internal experience without judgment, creating space between stimulus and reaction.

Other Therapies.

10. Life Coaching Therapy
Focus: The focus of life coaching is on helping individuals achieve personal goals, improve their life satisfaction, and maximize their potential. It is action-oriented and future-focused, often emphasizing goal-setting, personal development, and self-improvement. Life coaching therapy is designed to help clients navigate personal challenges, clarify their values, and create a roadmap for achieving specific life goals. Unlike traditional therapy, life coaching does not typically focus on treating mental health disorders but rather on fostering personal growth and accomplishment.How It’s Done: Life coaches work with clients to identify their personal or professional goals and the steps necessary to achieve them. Sessions often involve discussions around clarifying life purpose, developing strategies for overcoming obstacles, creating actionable plans, and boosting motivation. Coaches may use techniques like vision boards, goal-setting exercises, journaling, and mindfulness practices to help clients stay on track and build confidence. Coaching sessions are typically structured and can be either in-person or virtual. Life coaching is generally short-term, with a focus on immediate and future results rather than long-term exploration. Life coaching therapy can be particularly helpful for individuals looking to improve their careers, relationships, or overall life satisfaction, but it’s not designed for individuals with significant mental health issues (though it can complement traditional therapy). It empowers clients to become more proactive, gain clarity, and create the life they envision.

content:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is a form of psychotherapy that focuses on altering dysfunctional emotions, behaviors, and thoughts by challenging and replacing negative or irrational beliefs. Known for its "solution-focused" approach, CBT operates on the premise that thoughts and perceptions significantly influence behavior. At times, feelings of distress can distort one's perception of reality. CBT seeks to identify these harmful thoughts, assess their accuracy, and, when they are found to be unrealistic, provides strategies to challenge and overcome them.

CBT is suitable for individuals of all ages, children, adolescents, and adults, and has been shown to effectively address a wide range of conditions, including depression, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), eating disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and many others. Doctors and insurance providers often prefer CBT due to its proven effectiveness within a relatively short timeframe, typically ranging from 5 to 20 sessions. However, the exact duration can vary depending on the individual's needs. Research also indicates that CBT can be delivered successfully online, in addition to traditional face-to-face therapy.

Emotions, Thoughts, Behavior

CBT in Practice
CBT primarily focuses on present-day circumstances and emotions, rather than delving into childhood events. While a therapist may inquire about family history to gain a holistic understanding of the individual, the emphasis remains on the person's current thoughts and how they may be contributing to anxiety or distress. The therapist then encourages the person to challenge irrational beliefs, ruminations, or catastrophic thinking and to address concerns in a practical, solution-oriented manner.

For example, an individual frustrated by being single might be encouraged to take actionable steps while simultaneously questioning extreme or unfounded beliefs, such as "I will always be alone."

How Long Does CBT Take to Be Effective?
Typically, a CBT course consists of 5 to 20 weekly sessions, each lasting approximately 45 minutes. Treatment may continue with less frequent sessions as the individual practices their skills independently. The entire process generally lasts between 3 to 6 months, though it may extend longer if necessary. Throughout therapy, patients learn how to identify and challenge harmful thought patterns, replacing them with more realistic and healthier perspectives. Between sessions, patients may be given homework assignments, such as exercises to track their thoughts and apply newly acquired skills to real-life situations.

Why is CBT Effective?
CBT programs are structured and systematic, ensuring that individuals receive consistent "doses" of healthy thinking and behavior. For example, a person with depression may be asked to write down their thoughts when something upsetting occurs and then work with the therapist to assess the usefulness and accuracy of those thoughts. Repetition and focused practice are key components of CBT, as it centers on building new, positive habits—things that we may already know but need to remember and put into practice effectively. Moreover, CBT programs are designed to be standardized and tested, allowing the mental health field to determine which approaches are most effective, the time required, and the benefits that patients can expect.

What Conditions Can CBT Treat?
Initially developed to treat depression, CBT has been shown to be effective for a wide range of conditions, including anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), substance use disorders, and phobias. Additionally, various adaptations of CBT have been created to address insomnia and eating disorders. Beyond treating clinical conditions, CBT can also help individuals improve their relationships, happiness, and overall life satisfaction.

Clients explains her feeling (emotions, thoughts and behavior).

CBT and life coaches
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) techniques can be effectively utilized by life coaches, although it's important to note that life coaches are not licensed therapists and cannot officially diagnose or treat mental health conditions. However, many of the principles and strategies used in CBT align with life coaching practices aimed at personal growth, goal setting, and overcoming limiting beliefs. How Life Coaches Use CBT Techniques:

Identifying Negative Thought Patterns: Life coaches can help clients identify negative or irrational thought patterns that may be limiting their success or happiness. By using CBT techniques, they can assist clients in recognizing unhelpful beliefs and replacing them with more constructive ones.

Challenging Cognitive Distortions: Life coaches can guide clients in examining common cognitive distortions (e.g., all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophizing, overgeneralization) that might be affecting their ability to make progress toward their goals. Coaches can teach clients how to challenge these distortions and replace them with more realistic, balanced thoughts.

Goal Setting and Action Planning: CBT often involves setting specific, achievable goals and developing action plans to meet them. Life coaches can apply this approach by helping clients break down their larger goals into manageable steps, track progress, and stay motivated.

Behavioral Change: CBT emphasizes the connection between thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Life coaches can help clients modify unproductive behaviors by guiding them to identify the underlying thoughts and emotions that are influencing their actions. This helps clients create lasting behavioral change.

Building Self-Efficacy: CBT techniques are often used to increase self-efficacy—the belief that one can achieve their goals. Life coaches can use CBT to help clients boost their confidence by recognizing their strengths, identifying past successes, and fostering a growth mindset.

CBT in Practice

CBT primarily focuses on present-day circumstances and emotions, rather than delving into childhood events. While a therapist may inquire about family history to gain a holistic understanding of the individual, the emphasis remains on the person's current thoughts and how they may be contributing to anxiety or distress. The therapist then encourages the person to challenge irrational beliefs, ruminations, or catastrophic thinking and to address concerns in a practical, solution-oriented manner.

For example, an individual frustrated by being single might be encouraged to take actionable steps while simultaneously questioning extreme or unfounded beliefs, such as "I will always be alone."

How Long Does CBT Take to Be Effective?

Typically, a CBT course consists of 5 to 20 weekly sessions, each lasting approximately 45 minutes. Treatment may continue with less frequent sessions as the individual practices their skills independently. The entire process generally lasts between 3 to 6 months, though it may extend longer if necessary. Throughout therapy, patients learn how to identify and challenge harmful thought patterns, replacing them with more realistic and healthier perspectives. Between sessions, patients may be given homework assignments, such as exercises to track their thoughts and apply newly acquired skills to real-life situations.

Why is CBT Effective?

CBT programs are structured and systematic, ensuring that individuals receive consistent "doses" of healthy thinking and behavior. For example, a person with depression may be asked to write down their thoughts when something upsetting occurs and then work with the therapist to assess the usefulness and accuracy of those thoughts. Repetition and focused practice are key components of CBT, as it centers on building new, positive habits—things that we may already know but need to remember and put into practice effectively. Moreover, CBT programs are designed to be standardized and tested, allowing the mental health field to determine which approaches are most effective, the time required, and the benefits that patients can expect.

What Conditions Can CBT Treat?

Initially developed to treat depression, CBT has been shown to be effective for a wide range of conditions, including anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), substance use disorders, and phobias. Additionally, various adaptations of CBT have been created to address insomnia and eating disorders. Beyond treating clinical conditions, CBT can also help individuals improve their relationships, happiness, and overall life satisfaction.

Clients explains her feeling (emotions, thoughts and behavior).

CBT and life coaches

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) techniques can be effectively utilized by life coaches, although it's important to note that life coaches are not licensed therapists and cannot officially diagnose or treat mental health conditions. However, many of the principles and strategies used in CBT align with life coaching practices aimed at personal growth, goal setting, and overcoming limiting beliefs. How Life Coaches Use CBT Techniques:

Identifying Negative Thought Patterns: Life coaches can help clients identify negative or irrational thought patterns that may be limiting their success or happiness. By using CBT techniques, they can assist clients in recognizing unhelpful beliefs and replacing them with more constructive ones.

Challenging Cognitive Distortions: Life coaches can guide clients in examining common cognitive distortions (e.g., all-or-nothing thinking, catastrophizing, overgeneralization) that might be affecting their ability to make progress toward their goals. Coaches can teach clients how to challenge these distortions and replace them with more realistic, balanced thoughts.

Goal Setting and Action Planning: CBT often involves setting specific, achievable goals and developing action plans to meet them. Life coaches can apply this approach by helping clients break down their larger goals into manageable steps, track progress, and stay motivated.

Behavioral Change: CBT emphasizes the connection between thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Life coaches can help clients modify unproductive behaviors by guiding them to identify the underlying thoughts and emotions that are influencing their actions. This helps clients create lasting behavioral change.

Building Self-Efficacy: CBT techniques are often used to increase self-efficacy—the belief that one can achieve their goals. Life coaches can use CBT to help clients boost their confidence by recognizing their strengths, identifying past successes, and fostering a growth mindset.

content:
Wanting to help others is crucial for those aspiring to be coaches, but the personality traits of the coach play an equally significant role. In fact, a coach's personality can greatly influence the effectiveness of their support for clients. Since coaches often handle complex and challenging issues, certain traits are essential for them to not only cope but thrive in what can be a demanding profession. While some might think that offering good advice alone makes someone a great coach, successful coaches possess a range of qualities that go well beyond being articulate.

Compassionate and Non-Judgmental
In order for a client to feel comfortable opening up to his coach, the coach should display compassion for the client's problems and the client should feel that he won't be judged. A coach shouldn't operate as if he is a superior working with an inferior person; he should put his own values and beliefs aside and respect a client's beliefs, even if they conflict with his own. A coach should be able to communicate both verbally and non-verbally that he is someone the client can trust. If a client trusts his coach enough to be real with him, then the coaches will better understand the client's problems and be able to help him find lasting solutions.

Stable and Secure
A coach should be stable and consistent. His office should be a place of security for the client. A client may be suffering because he does not have consistency or stability within himself if he suffers from a psychiatric problem. Or, a client may need therapy because his home life is unstable. Finding stability in the coach office can play a key role in a client becoming stable.

Honest
An authentic and honest coach plays a key role in his client's recovery. Often, a coach will inadvertently become a role model for his client. That means the coach should conduct his personal and professional lives with honesty and integrity. The coach should exhibit traits that are good to emulate and will help the client succeed in his own life. 

Skeptical
A good degree of skepticism also plays an important role in therapy. A coach shouldn't believe everything the client says without any evidence. Clients sometimes lie to hide a truth that embarrasses them or in order to avoid personal responsibility. Clients may even deceive themselves. A coach needs to think critically and see beyond the surface.

Intelligent and Inquisitive
A coach who is intelligent and inquisitive will stay updated on the latest research and treatment plans so that he can help his clients in the best way possible. This type of coach will listen carefully to the client, research the client's issues and help explain why the client is experiencing symptoms and what treatments will work best. A coach who isn't willing to do research on his own and continue learning will not be able to provide his clients with the best treatment options possible.

Ability to Empathize
Empathy is an important characteristic to being a good coach. People come to therapy with all sorts of emotional and mental concerns, which may cause them to feel vulnerable. A callous coach may be ineffective in gaining the trust needed to help resolve the presenting issues. Simply nodding or saying, "I understand" may put a client at ease.

Ability to Observe Clearly
An effective coach identifies trends of negative behavioral and thinking patterns by simply listening to and observing his clients. The inflection in the client's voice and her body language provides information to the observant coach. For example, if a couple comes in and the husband angrily says he thinks the marriage is fine, while sitting as far from his spouse as possible, the coach knows that everything is not "fine."

Ability to Listen Actively
Through active listening, effective coach guide clients to finding their own answers, but listening is a learned skill. Good coaches are able to listen without interrupting or offering advice. During active listening, counselors are not only hearing the client's words but are also understanding the unstated message behind the words. Asking the right questions at the right time is also an important part of active listening. 

Ability to Organize and Use Time-management Strategies
Coaches are responsible for keeping track of paperwork, including insurance documents and case notes for each client. The counselor must have an organized system of retention that protects client confidentiality while keeping the notes at hand and retrievable. They must also keep an accurate schedule to avoid booking multiple clients for the same time slot and to keep appointments on track.

Compassion
Compassion and empathy are two of the most important personal qualities of any coach. The ability to convey compassion and empathy is often referred to as "starting where your client is at." A genuine desire to help others and to the ability to understand and relate to their pain and struggles is necessary in order to help patients feel that you're truly invested in helping them solve their problems. You should be able to put yourself in someone else's shoes while you maintain professional boundaries.

Inquisitiveness
Inquisitiveness in psychology might be defined as a desire to understand the inner workings of the human mind and to discover why people act and think the way they do. Being inquisitive means that you are curious and keen to understand why your patients make certain choices and what is causing the dysfunction in their lives. Curiosity and interest are especially important for coaches who encounter patients who have a different value system than their own, according to Shannon Vincent Wilde in her dissertation, "Value Conflicts in Psychotherapy." You should have a willingness to learn more about your patients' values and beliefs instead of trying to impose your own beliefs on others.

Self-Awareness
Coaches need to be self-aware and have a good understanding of their own mind before they can truly help others. If you don't have the ability to self-reflect and understand your own motivations, you might be tempted to jump to conclusions or subconsciously superimpose your own issues on your patients. A deeper understanding of who you are is crucial if you want to become a better coach.

Communication Skills
Excellent communication skills are critical for every coach, since they spend much of their time talking with and listening to patients, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. You should be able to tease out the underlying messages in what your clients say, be perceptive to non-verbal forms of communication, such as eye contact or physical postures, be able to listen for long periods of time without becoming bored or impatient, and be able to reflect back to your clients the significant thoughts and feelings that you observe.

Communication is very important for a coach

Do's and Don'ts

Do's
Don'ts

If you have a client, just enjoy and see the beauty of your job. You are helping people, and you can make a difference in somebodies' life.
Never prescribe and/or give advice about medication

If you are new and you are just starting, be open and honest to your client about your experience.
When clients have a severe issue like thoughts about suicide and self-harm, don’t try to do any treatment if the client is in a dangerous position

Be very clear and honest to your clients about your background. A coach is not the same as a psychologist. Know your rights.
Clients are normally in a difficult time of their life. They are fragile and they put a lot of trust and hope in the coach. When seeing clients in a professional setting, keep a professional distance!!! Don’t touch clients!!! Don’t talk about your own private life!!!! Don’t become friends during treatment or see people outside the session!!! When the treatment is finished and there is no client-coach situation anymore, you can have closer contact.

Remember, you have always the right to refuse a client or to stop the support
As a coach, you are not able to diagnose people! Only mental hospitals can diagnose people in Vietnam!

After this course
You finished the general coaching course. Now it is time to professionalize yourself in a preferred area. Choose an area that you have affection for. For example, if you like children, you may want to follow a course in children. Some people choose a course that will probably deliver them a lot of work, for example a sleep coach. People are more and more aware of the importance of sleeping. At the same time, people are more stressed and showing more difficulties in maintaining good sleep habits. A sleeping coach could be a valuable and important job. For the latest updates, please visit the website, course overview. 

Information about the follow up course. 

Each course is given by a qualified teacher / therapist.

You meet with your teacher ones a week online on Zalo.

Your teacher is also available two times a week to answer your questions.

If you successfully finish the course you will receive a certificate.

A weekly assessment (homework) is given and checked  by your teacher.

After signing up for any course, we will keep you up to date about new research and the newest updates about psychology.

We prepare you to be an independent life coach by providing the tools, knowledge, and support you need to build a successful practice. 

One of our students started her own practice.
Starting my journey as a life coach has been one of the most rewarding decisions I've ever made. After years of feeling unfulfilled in my previous career, I took a leap of faith and decided to help others navigate their lives and find clarity. Becoming a life coach has allowed me to not only assist others in achieving their goals but also to rediscover my own purpose.

The most beautiful part of having my own practice is the freedom it offers. I can set my schedule, choose the clients I work with, and create an environment where I can truly focus on the needs of each individual. My work is no longer just a job; it’s a passion. Every session, every conversation, is an opportunity to witness someone's transformation, and that sense of fulfillment is unparalleled.

Building my own practice hasn’t come without its challenges, there were moments of doubt and uncertainty. However, the ability to structure my own business, create my own methods, and witness my clients' growth has made every challenge worth it. I am not just a coach; I am a guide, a partner in my clients’ journeys, and I get to help them unlock their potential every day.

Having my own practice allows me to make a real difference in the lives of others while also achieving a work-life balance that brings me true happiness. It’s a beautiful, fulfilling career where I can combine my passion for helping others with the flexibility and satisfaction of owning my own business.

Certificate
Congratulations! You’ve made it, and I hope this journey has deepened your understanding of psychology in meaningful ways. Through your dedication, energy, and commitment to completing the course, you’ve earned a certificate (see my certificates, after finishing this unit). The value you assign to this certificate is entirely up to you, but it represents the completion of one of the best coaching courses available.

Psychologist Vietnam is not just an organization; it is a nationally recognized entity, and now, you are part of it, even if indirectly. But there’s more! With this certificate, you gain the opportunity to enroll in additional courses to further specialize in specific areas of coaching. After completing these advanced courses, you’ll be able to work with real clients, helping and supporting others in meaningful ways.

We hope you display this certificate proudly, perhaps hanging it in your office as a testament to your achievement. As an added service, we offer the option to receive a hard copy of your certificate on high-quality paper, complete with the Psychologist Vietnam stamp and signature, for an additional 200,000 VND. If you’d like to request a hard copy, please email us at info@bridge-academy.vn.

Once again, congratulations on this significant milestone!

content:
Insomnia Immediate Action: 
Turn off all screens 1 hour before bed, keep your bedroom cool and dark, and cut off caffeine after lunch.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends.

Right after waking, open your curtains and step outside for 10–15 minutes of natural sunlight.

Build a sleep wind-down routine every night: dim the lights, take a warm shower, then spend 10–15 minutes reading a book or stretching gently. Avoid stimulants and heavy meals in the afternoon and evening. Instead, drink calming herbal tea like chamomile after 6 PM.

Depression Immediate Action: 
Reach out to someone you trust, get professional support, and set just one small task to complete each morning.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Take a 20-minute walk outdoors, even if it's just around your block.

Focus on your senses: What do you see? Hear? Smell? Write down 3 small wins at the end of your day, even if they feel minor (e.g., "I got out of bed," "I drank water").

Schedule one activity you used to enjoy (e.g., music, drawing, playing a game) and do it for 15–30 minutes, even if motivation is low.

Anxiety Immediate Action: 
Pause and take 3 deep breaths, bring awareness to your surroundings, and reduce caffeine and screen time.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Start your day with 10 minutes of breathing or mindfulness. Sit comfortably, inhale for 4 seconds, exhale for 6.

Limit news and social media to set time blocks. Try 15 minutes in the morning and 15 in the evening only.

Write a list of 3 small tasks in the morning and check them off as you go. This builds momentum and reduces overwhelm.

Brain Diseases (Dementia, Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s) Immediate Action: 
Stick to a simple daily routine, label important items (e.g., drawers, remotes), and keep the living space clean and clutter-free.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Do gentle brain games for 15–20 minutes (crosswords, matching games, memory cards).

Encourage light movement or stretching, even seated exercises help maintain coordination and circulation.

Have a short chat daily with someone familiar, in person or by phone. Even a 5-minute check-in helps reduce confusion and isolation.

Dyslexia Immediate Action: 
Use tools like text-to-speech apps, audiobooks, and colored overlays to make reading easier and less stressful.

 Top 3 Daily Activities:

Practice reading along with audio support, just 10 minutes a day helps build confidence.

Use color-coded flashcards or sticky notes to organize ideas or break down tasks.

Read aloud together in a low-pressure setting, like bedtime or after dinner, to improve rhythm and comfort.

Male Sexual Problems Immediate Action: 
Let go of performance pressure. Focus on connection, not outcomes. Therapy can help with stress and body confidence.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Do 10–15 minutes of daily relaxation, like deep breathing or meditation to reduce anxiety.

Improve physical health with movement, sleep, and hydration. A brisk walk or workout helps circulation and mood.

Have honest conversations with your partner, share your feelings without shame or pressure.

Female Sexual Problems Immediate Action: 
Give yourself permission to slow down. Focus on emotional safety and comfort. Explore therapy if needed.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Make time for daily self-care: a relaxing bath, gentle stretching, or skin care.

Reconnect with your body without pressure. Keep a private journal to track emotions, thoughts, and what your body needs each day.

Practice mindful breathing for 5–10 minutes to release tension and increase body awareness.

Eating Disorder Immediate Action: 
Avoid mirrors, unfollow harmful social media accounts, and commit to eating at regular times—even without hunger.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Eat 3 meals + 2 snacks daily, use a meal plan or timer if needed.

Use post-meal distraction tools: puzzles, drawing, a calming playlist.

Write one kind or neutral thought about your body each day,focus on function, not appearance.

Stress Immediate Action: 
Pause. Take 5 slow breaths, drink water, and write down what’s truly urgent (not everything is!).

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Take 2–3 stretch breaks per day, especially after screen time.

Do a 5-minute grounding technique: notice 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste.

Celebrate 3 small wins at night, even if they’re tiny—"I replied to that email," "I asked for help," "I rested."

Burnout Immediate Action: 
Step back from what's draining you. Say “no” to non-essential tasks. Rest isn’t a luxury, it’s a must.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Do one thing just for you each day, even 15 minutes: music, nature, a nap, or quiet time.

Take short screen breaks every 90 minutes go outside, stretch, breathe.

Journal energy levels daily: What gave you energy? What drained you? Use it to set limits tomorrow.

Lack of Motivation Immediate Action: 
Break your task into one micro-step. Start with just 2 minutes, even brushing your teeth or sending 1 text counts.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

List 3 simple tasks for the day (tiny = better). Crossing them off builds momentum.

Do something physical, like a 3-minute dance break, a walk, or jumping jacks, motion boosts motivation.

Play upbeat music or a short podcast to shift your energy.

Tourette Syndrome Immediate Action: 
Take off the pressure to “hide” your tics. Focus on stress relief, not suppression.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Get daily movement, walking, dancing, or sports helps regulate excess energy.

Use deep breathing when tics feel intense. A few minutes can calm the body.

Keep a tic journal to track patterns and triggers, this helps plan your day better.

Autism Immediate Action: 
Honor your need for structure, quiet, and routine. Say no to overstimulation when you can.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Use a visual schedule with pictures, colors, or checklists to reduce anxiety.

Engage in sensory-friendly self-soothing, weighted blankets, soft textures, or calming sounds.

Spend time with a favorite interest, it's not a "waste of time," it’s joy and comfort.

ADHD Immediate Action: 
Use phone alarms or sticky notes. Break tasks into tiny chunks. Remove visual clutter from your workspace.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

 Use the Pomodoro method: 25 minutes focus, 5 minutes break. Repeat.

 Pick just 1 main goal per day and write it where you’ll see it.

 Get short bursts of movement every hour, stretching, pacing, or stepping outside helps reset focus.

Stuttering Immediate Action: 
Talk slowly and breathe deeply. Take pressure off being “perfectly fluent.” Progress happens with patience.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Practice speaking in front of a mirror or record yourself in your own time.

Do daily breathing or vocal warm-ups, even just 5 minutes.

Read aloud something fun or familiar, at your own pace.

Addiction Immediate Action: 
Cut off access to triggers or substances. Get help, don’t wait for a “rock bottom.” Recovery starts with one choice.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Check in daily with a support system, group, sponsor, friend, therapist.

Use urge surfing, wait out cravings like a wave. They pass.

Journal your emotions or track triggers, and try CBT-based self-talk to challenge them.

Aggression Immediate Action: 
Step away from the situation, take 10 deep breaths, splash water on your face. Give your body a reset.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

Do physical activity every day, walking, hitting a punching bag, or push-ups to release energy.

Keep an anger journal: What triggered me? What did I need instead?

Use 4–7–8 breathing to calm down fast: inhale 4 sec, hold 7 sec, exhale 8 sec.

Insomnia Immediate Action:

Turn off all screens 1 hour before bed, keep your bedroom cool and dark, and cut off caffeine after lunch.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends.
  • Right after waking, open your curtains and step outside for 10–15 minutes of natural sunlight.
  • Build a sleep wind-down routine every night: dim the lights, take a warm shower, then spend 10–15 minutes reading a book or stretching gently. Avoid stimulants and heavy meals in the afternoon and evening. Instead, drink calming herbal tea like chamomile after 6 PM.

Depression Immediate Action:

Reach out to someone you trust, get professional support, and set just one small task to complete each morning.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Take a 20-minute walk outdoors, even if it's just around your block.
  • Focus on your senses: What do you see? Hear? Smell? Write down 3 small wins at the end of your day, even if they feel minor (e.g., "I got out of bed," "I drank water").
  • Schedule one activity you used to enjoy (e.g., music, drawing, playing a game) and do it for 15–30 minutes, even if motivation is low.

Anxiety Immediate Action:

Pause and take 3 deep breaths, bring awareness to your surroundings, and reduce caffeine and screen time.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Start your day with 10 minutes of breathing or mindfulness. Sit comfortably, inhale for 4 seconds, exhale for 6.
  • Limit news and social media to set time blocks. Try 15 minutes in the morning and 15 in the evening only.
  • Write a list of 3 small tasks in the morning and check them off as you go. This builds momentum and reduces overwhelm.

Brain Diseases (Dementia, Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s) Immediate Action:

Stick to a simple daily routine, label important items (e.g., drawers, remotes), and keep the living space clean and clutter-free.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Do gentle brain games for 15–20 minutes (crosswords, matching games, memory cards).
  • Encourage light movement or stretching, even seated exercises help maintain coordination and circulation.
  • Have a short chat daily with someone familiar, in person or by phone. Even a 5-minute check-in helps reduce confusion and isolation.

Dyslexia Immediate Action:

Use tools like text-to-speech apps, audiobooks, and colored overlays to make reading easier and less stressful.

 Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Practice reading along with audio support, just 10 minutes a day helps build confidence.
  • Use color-coded flashcards or sticky notes to organize ideas or break down tasks.
  • Read aloud together in a low-pressure setting, like bedtime or after dinner, to improve rhythm and comfort.

Male Sexual Problems Immediate Action:

Let go of performance pressure. Focus on connection, not outcomes. Therapy can help with stress and body confidence.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Do 10–15 minutes of daily relaxation, like deep breathing or meditation to reduce anxiety.
  • Improve physical health with movement, sleep, and hydration. A brisk walk or workout helps circulation and mood.
  • Have honest conversations with your partner, share your feelings without shame or pressure.

Female Sexual Problems Immediate Action:

Give yourself permission to slow down. Focus on emotional safety and comfort. Explore therapy if needed.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Make time for daily self-care: a relaxing bath, gentle stretching, or skin care.
  • Reconnect with your body without pressure. Keep a private journal to track emotions, thoughts, and what your body needs each day.
  • Practice mindful breathing for 5–10 minutes to release tension and increase body awareness.

Eating Disorder Immediate Action:

Avoid mirrors, unfollow harmful social media accounts, and commit to eating at regular times—even without hunger.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Eat 3 meals + 2 snacks daily, use a meal plan or timer if needed.
  • Use post-meal distraction tools: puzzles, drawing, a calming playlist.
  • Write one kind or neutral thought about your body each day,focus on function, not appearance.

Stress Immediate Action:

Pause. Take 5 slow breaths, drink water, and write down what’s truly urgent (not everything is!).

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Take 2–3 stretch breaks per day, especially after screen time.
  • Do a 5-minute grounding technique: notice 5 things you can see, 4 you can touch, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste.
  • Celebrate 3 small wins at night, even if they’re tiny—"I replied to that email," "I asked for help," "I rested."

Burnout Immediate Action:

Step back from what's draining you. Say “no” to non-essential tasks. Rest isn’t a luxury, it’s a must.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Do one thing just for you each day, even 15 minutes: music, nature, a nap, or quiet time.
  • Take short screen breaks every 90 minutes go outside, stretch, breathe.
  • Journal energy levels daily: What gave you energy? What drained you? Use it to set limits tomorrow.

Lack of Motivation Immediate Action:

Break your task into one micro-step. Start with just 2 minutes, even brushing your teeth or sending 1 text counts.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • List 3 simple tasks for the day (tiny = better). Crossing them off builds momentum.
  • Do something physical, like a 3-minute dance break, a walk, or jumping jacks, motion boosts motivation.
  • Play upbeat music or a short podcast to shift your energy.

Take off the pressure to “hide” your tics. Focus on stress relief, not suppression.

Top 3 Daily Activities:

  • Get daily movement, walking, dancing, or sports helps regulate excess energy.
  • Use deep breathing when tics feel intense. A few minutes can calm the body.
  • Keep a tic journal to track patterns and triggers, this helps plan your day better.

title: Acknowledgement
about: Congratulations on completing this course to become a life coach! I am incredibly proud of you for reaching this milestone. You've worked hard, and your dedication has brought you to this point. I sincerely hope that you will continue your journey by enrolling in further courses
content:
Congratulations on completing this course to become a life coach! I am incredibly proud of you for reaching this milestone. You've worked hard, and your dedication has brought you to this point. I sincerely hope that you will continue your journey by enrolling in further courses to deepen your understanding of the field of psychology. The more you learn, the better equipped you'll be to not only understand psychology on a deeper level, but also to offer insightful and valuable advice to those around you. As a life coach, the most rewarding gift you can give is the ability to help others transform and grow.

You are now part of a special group who have completed this course and will continue to pursue further knowledge and expertise. I’m thrilled to know that many of you will be involved in follow-up courses, and I look forward to seeing you all in real life. A heartfelt thank you goes to everyone who has supported me in my mission to establish a mental health organization in Vietnam. Currently, I’m incredibly grateful for the 25 mental health professionals who are connected with our organization, our 20,000 followers on Facebook, our clients who trust in our expertise and professionalism, and many other people who supported me in this jurney. Together, we are making a meaningful impact. In addition to our professional services, we run a suicide prevention hotline, a supportive forum, and collaborate with an orphanage to provide charity support.

As a personal note, please don’t hesitate to reach out to me at merijn@psychologistvietnam.com. While I may not always be able to respond immediately, I guarantee I will read every message.Thank you once again for your dedication, and I wish you the best of luck as you move forward in your life coaching career. Be the own CEO of your own life.

Lets make mental health count in Vietnam!!!!

Warm regards,Merijn Mattheijssen
Founder of Psychologist Vietnam
